item.title: [1.8] MET inhibition exploits conserved regulatory dependencies in malignant rhabdoid tumors
item.description:
Malignant rhabdoid tumors (MRTs) are lethal, yet genomically simple childhood cancers characterised by universal SWI/SNF dysregulation. Despite this shared molecular framework, the regulatory programs sustaining MRTs and how they wire actionable dependencies, remain poorly defined. Here, we integrated single-cell multi-omic profiling and spatial transcriptomics across anatomically and molecularly diverse MRTs, generating a comprehensive multimodal MRT dataset at single-cell resolution. We leveraged this resource to identify candidate tumor-specific dependencies, which were subsequently functionally validated in vitro and in vivo in matched patient-derived models. We found that distinct malignant subpopulations are spatially patterned in complex environmentally shaped topologies, consistent with reciprocal interactions with stromal and immune compartments contributing to intratumoral transcriptional diversity. We identified recurrent transcriptional metaprograms conserved across patients and molecular subtypes, including a previously undescribed shared core rhabdoid program, as well as a metaprogram characterized by extracellular matrix interactions, and preferentially localized in tumor-stroma intermixed neighborhoods, supporting identification of niche conditioning cues. Mechanistically, we identified regulatory wiring driving these metaprograms, with the core shared rhabdoid programme coordinated by a circuit centred on TCF12, ZNF148 and CHD2. Guided by target nominations from our integrated analyses, we performed a curated drug screen using patient-derived MRT models and validated HGF/MET signaling as a selective vulnerability in extrarenal rhabdoid tumors. Pharmacologic MET inhibition was cytotoxic in sensitive models and induced a complete response in vivo using a clinically approved compound. Importantly, MET expression in primary tumors correlated with response, supporting biomarker-guided patient stratification for immediate clinical translation. Collectively, our findings define the molecular architecture of MRTs, reveal conserved regulatory programs beyond anatomical and molecular subtypes, and highlight a targetable signaling axis with immediate translational potential, establishing a framework for precision therapy in this lethal pediatric malignancy.

item.title: [1.9] Glioblastoma model mouse rescue from mortality by brain-targeted catalytically-enhanced angiotensin-converting enzyme 2 mutant-antibody fusion protein
item.description:
We have discovered that an engineered angiotensin-converting enzyme 2 (ACE2)-brain-targeted antibody fusion protein, referred to as ACE2dm-s1, improves survival of CT-2A xenograft glioblastoma (GBM) model mice when administered in combination with a small molecule STING agonist cancer therapeutic. Particularly striking about these survival results is that prior efforts that used losartan, a small molecule angiotensin receptor antagonist that acts on the same Renin-Angiotensin System (RAS) axis that is affected by the action of ACE2dm-s1, showed that this small molecule provided no survival benefit when used as an element of combination therapy in the same CT-2A GBM model used in our experiments. The improved CT-2A mouse survival, which was not observed for ACE2dm-s1 or STING agonist monotherapy, combines with our flow cytometry study results that revealed an ACE2dm-s1-mediated shift of brain immune cell populations toward an anti-tumoral composition to establish ACE2dm-s1's utility as a tumor microenvironment (TME) modulator that could serve as an adjuvant in increasing the efficacy of wide range of cancer treatment modalities including chemotherapeutic agents, immune checkpoint inhibitors, and CAR-T cells.

item.title: [1.9] Alpha-aminoadipate in the saccharopine pathway promotes cancer metastasis through sumoylation of transcription machinery
item.description:
Despite studies linking metabolism and cancer, our understanding of the metabolite network that drives metastasis remains incomplete. Through a metabolic RNAi-based screen for cell invasion, we identify alpha-aminoadipate (2-AAA), the intermediate metabolite of aminoadipic semialdehyde synthase (AASS) in the saccharopine pathway, as a common pivotal factor in metastasis of human cancers. Metabolite-protein connectivity mapping reveals that 2-AAA binds to SAE1, a crucial component of the SUMO-activating enzyme E1, and enhances SAE1 recruitment to UBA2, facilitating sumoylation. 2-AAA-mediated sumoylation of the RNA polymerase subunit POLR2A then partially promotes cancer cell invasion by inducing the expression of metastasis-promoting genes, including SPG11 and KCTD7. Targeting AASS with cetalkonium chloride, a newly identified small molecule inhibitor against AASS, attenuates cancer cell invasion and tumor metastasis. Our study highlights the mechanism by which metastasis is mediated by metabolite-driven sumoylation and indicates AASS as an effective therapeutic target for mitigating metastatic cancer progression. The role of metabolism in metastasis remains unclear. Here, a metabolic RNAi-based screen for cell invasion and metabolite-protein connectivity mapping reveals a mechanism by which sumoylation driven by alpha-aminoadipate, the intermediate metabolite of aminoadipic semialdehyde synthase, drives metastasis.

item.title: [1.6] Death pathway plasticity in therapy resistance: mechanistic switches and translational opportunities
item.description:
Regulated cell death (RCD) programs in cancer have traditionally been framed as discrete pathways defined by signature effectors, including caspases (apoptosis), RIPK1–RIPK3–MLKL (necroptosis), gasdermins (pyroptosis), lipid peroxidation control nodes (ferroptosis), PARP1–AIF/MIF (parthanatos), and FDX1-dependent lipoylation stress (cuproptosis). Here, we advance an integrated view in which these programs function as a configurable decision network rather than isolated routes. Therapeutic and microenvironmental inputs, such as death ligands, chemoradiotherapy, targeted agents, PARP inhibition, copper ionophores, nutrient/oxidative stress, extracellular matrix detachment, and cytotoxic T-cell pressure, converge on shared hub modules that act as rheostats, routing cells toward distinct execution outcomes or into drug-tolerant persister states. This circuit-level framing explains context-dependent switching and mixed phenotypes, including caspase-8/c-FLIP control of apoptosis–necroptosis, caspase–gasdermin coupling of apoptosis–pyroptosis, and metabolic–redox tuning of ferroptosis susceptibility via SLC7A11–GPX4–ACSL4–FSP1 and autophagy-linked lipid/iron handling. We outline a biomarker and functional assay framework to map tumor death wiring from biopsies and organoid challenges, enabling rational combination strategies that exploit death program plasticity while anticipating resistance and inflammatory toxicities.

item.title: [1.9] PD-L1 is associated with metabolic adaptation and mitochondrial remodeling in NSCLC cells
item.description:
Tumor metabolism is governed by a complex network of processes that can influence immune evasion. Metabolic dysregulation in tumor cells can lead to the accumulation of metabolites that may influence immune cell function. However, the relationship between PD-L1 expression and tumor cell metabolism remains incompletely understood. Here, we report that PD-L1 expression in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) cells is associated with increased endocytic activity and altered metabolic flux, particularly in the tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle. PD-L1 expression is aleo associated with mitochondrial remodeling, including alterations in proteins involved in mitochondrial fusion and fission and in mitochondrial respiratory chain components. Integrated multi-omics analyses further identified differential H3K9me3 patterns associated with differences in PD-L1 expression status, including differential H3K9me3 patterns at the PTPRN2 locus. Collectively, our findings suggest that differences in PD-L1 expression status are associated with metabolic, mitochondrial, and epigenetic alterations in NSCLC cells.

item.title: [2.0] Perioperative ivonescimab with or without chemotherapy in resectable non-small cell lung cancer: a phase 2 trial
item.description:
Resectable non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) carries a high risk of postoperative recurrence, underscoring the need for effective perioperative therapies. This nonrandomized, noncomparative phase 2 trial evaluated neoadjuvant ivonescimab monotherapy (cohort 1) or in combination with chemotherapy (cohort 2), followed by surgery and adjuvant ivonescimab. In cohort 2, the major pathological response (MPR) rate was 70.1% (47/67; 95% confidence interval (CI) = 57.7–80.7); the lower bound of the 80% two-sided CI exceeded the historical control rate of 41% and the primary endpoint was met. The MPR rate in cohort 1 was 60.0% (6/10; 95% CI = 26.2–87.8). Among patients who achieved MPR, 83.3% (5/6) in cohort 1 and 97.9% (46/47) in cohort 2 had residual viable tumor (RVT) of ≤5%, respectively. Grade 3 or higher treatment-related adverse events (AEs) occurred in 36.4% (4/11) patients in cohort 1 and 30.4% (24/79) of those in cohort 2, with no grade 3 or higher hemorrhage or treatment-related death. Treatment-related surgery delay occurred in one (1.3%) patient. Surgery-related AEs related to ivonescimab occurred in 10.0% (1/10) and 10.4% (7/67) patients in the two cohorts, respectively, with no grade 3 or higher events reported. These data support perioperative ivonescimab with or without chemotherapy as a promising strategy for resectable NSCLC. ClinicalTrials.gov identifier: NCT05247684 . In a nonrandomized phase 2 trial, patients with resectable non-small cell lung cancer received perioperative ivonescimab as monotherapy or with chemotherapy, leading to encouraging pathological response rates in both cohorts, and sustained circulating tumor DNA negativity throughout neoadjuvant therapy may be predictive of response.

item.title: [1.9] Decoding the regulatory programs governing glioblastoma plasticity
item.description:
Glioblastoma is incurable and resistant to therapy despite genomic stability under treatment1–8, suggesting that non-genetic cellular plasticity is a central driver of progression. Whether such plasticity reflects stochastic state switching or is governed by predictable gene regulation has remained unclear9–13. Here we introduce scDORI (single-cell deep multi-omic regulatory inference)—a deep-learning framework that infers enhancer-driven gene-regulatory networks at single-cell resolution—and apply it to single-nucleus multiome profiles of more than one million cells from primary glioblastomas. Integrating computational inference with systematic perturbation screens across patient-derived models, we show that a structured regulatory program with an asymmetric interplay of activators and repressors governs cellular plasticity in glioblastoma. The resulting transition landscape is hierarchical and predictable, but permits cross-lineage trajectories that are absent from normal neurodevelopment. Within this landscape, low-plasticity states such as the neuronal-like state are not stable differentiation end points but actively maintained configurations, stabilized by a network of safeguard repressors that silence alternative fates. We identify MYT1L as the dominant member of this network, and show that it binds to and represses master regulators of every alternative state to consolidate neuronal-like identity. MYT1L restricted plasticity even under standard-of-care therapy and suppressed tumour growth and invasion in vivo. Conversely, loss of MYT1L reactivated plasticity and accelerated malignant features, indicating that low-plasticity identity requires continuous repression. These findings reframe malignant cell state stability as a balance between activation and continuous repression, and nominate safeguard repressors as candidate therapeutic targets that are distinct from differentiation-inducing activators, with potential relevance across cancers in which phenotypic switching drives therapy resistance. Multi-omic analyses of cells from patients with glioblastoma (GB) provide insight into the role of non-genetic cellular plasticity in disease progression, showing that state stability in GB cells is controlled by a network of interacting activators and repressors.

item.title: [1.5] Early Progression Cells mark a stem-like state associated with pancreatic cancer initiation and progression
item.description:
Pancreatic cancer is deemed to progress from microscopic pancreatic intraepithelial neoplasia (PanINs). However, low grade PanINs are frequently detected in the general population without presentation or increased risk of developing cancer, suggesting that many PanINs never progress to tumours. What precisely characterises PanINs that develop into tumours is insufficiently understood. Using a mouse model where pancreatitis-induced tissue injury promotes pancreatic cancer from rare KrasG12D cells, we identify Early Progression Cells (EPCs) as a new entity, a novel population of cancer stem-like cells. Transcriptomic analyses illustrate EPCs as stress-adapted, inflammation responsive stem cells that also upregulate gene programmes indicative of microenvironment remodelling. Using identified EPC protein markers, we show that EPCs are prevalent in early metaplastic stages and in PanIN progression from low grade to high grade but are rarer in tumours. PanIN- and tumour-derived sphere and organoid assays demonstrate that EPCs possess all characteristics of stem cells in vitro and are dependent on Nupr1 stress response pathways for survival and growth. We identify APP-CD74 as a novel cell-cell interaction pathway between EPCs and neighbouring epithelial cells in PanINs and tumours. Inhibition of CD74 activity in vitro induces high-grade PanIN organoid death, suggesting EPCs are critical for high-grade PanINs. Using spatial transcriptomics of human samples, we detect gene signatures of EPCs in distinct regions of human PanIN and PDAC tissues, including APP-CD74 interactions, providing compelling evidence that EPCs are relevant to human disease. Further understanding of EPC biology will likely uncover new knowledge on why rare PanINs progress towards tumours.

item.title: [1.5] Coupled Modeling of Tumor Volume and ctDNA Dynamics in HPV-Associated Anal Squamous Cell Carcinoma
item.description:
Response to anti-PD-1 immunotherapy in advanced HPV-associated anal squamous cell carcinoma (ASCC) varies and is assessed by infrequent imaging that lags behind tumor biology. Circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) can be sampled frequently and reflects near-real-time tumor activity yet is rarely built into mechanistic models of treatment response. Using longitudinal tumor volume and HPV ctDNA from 26 patients treated with pembrolizumab, we found that baseline ctDNA scores tracked tumor burden but did not distinguish responders from non-responders, whereas ctDNA after one treatment cycle had a higher relative decrease in responders, six weeks before the next scan. We developed an ordinary differential equation model linking tumor volume to the ctDNA released by tumor cells. Sensitivity, identifiability, and model-selection analyses reduced it to two patient-specific parameters, proliferation and shedding rates, which reproduced individual volume and ctDNA trajectories, including a transient ctDNA spike at treatment onset. Proliferation was faster in non-responders. This framework supports model-based, ctDNA-guided monitoring of immunotherapy response.

item.title: [2.1] AMD1-driven MTA production sustains chemoresistance by rewiring PMN-MDSC immunosuppression
item.description:
Chemoresistance reflects both tumor cell-intrinsic adaptation and remodeling of the immune microenvironment. However, the mechanisms by which chemoresistant tumor cells orchestrate and sustain an immunosuppressive microenvironment remain poorly understood. Here, we demonstrate that chemoresistant tumors exhibit marked accumulation of polymorphonuclear myeloid-derived suppressor cells (PMN-MDSCs), which exert potent immunosuppressive effects on CD8+T cells and are critical for drug resistance. Metabolomic profiling reveals that resistant tumor cells release the metabolite 5'-methylthioadenosine (MTA). MTA enhances the immunosuppressive function of PMN-MDSCs by bolstering JAK-STAT3 signaling. Mechanistically, MTA binds to the protein tyrosine phosphatase PTPN2 to block its phosphatase activity, thereby potentiating activation of JAK-STAT3 signaling pathway. Moreover, we uncover that adenosylmethionine decarboxylase 1 (AMD1) is the key metabolic determinant of MTA accumulation in chemoresistant tumor cells. Genetic or pharmacological AMD1 inhibition significantly decreases MTA level, diminishes PMN-MDSC immunosuppressive function, and re-sensitizes the resistant tumors to chemotherapy and immunotherapy. Our findings identify MTA as an important metabolic link between chemoresistant tumor cells and PMN-MDSCs to sustain immunosuppression and therapeutic resistance. Targeting AMD1-dependent MTA production represents a valuable strategy for overcoming chemo-immunotherapy resistance.

item.title: [1.9] Preliminary results and clinical experiences of [177Lu]Lu-FAP-2286 for brain metastases in advanced lung cancer
item.description:
Brain metastases in advanced lung cancer present a therapeutic challenge with limited effective options. Fibroblast activation protein (FAP) is overexpressed in cancer-associated fibroblasts within brain metastatic lesions, making it a promising target for radionuclide therapy. This prospective study evaluated the intracranial efficacy and safety of peptide-targeted radionuclide therapy (PTRT) with [177Lu]Lu-FAP-2286 in 14 patients with FAP-expressing advanced lung cancer and radiologically confirmed brain metastases who had failed prior treatments. Patients received [177Lu]Lu-FAP-2286 (7.4 GBq/cycle, ≥ 2 cycles). Intracranial objective response rate was 57.1% and disease control rate was 92.9% by RECIST 1.1, with a metabolic response rate of 64.3% by PERCIST 1.0. Median overall survival was 11.0 months and median progression-free survival was 8.0 months. Patients achieving metabolic response had significantly longer survival. Neurological symptoms and brain-specific quality of life improved significantly, and no grade III/IV adverse events occurred. These findings suggest that systemic [177Lu]Lu-FAP-2286 PTRT is safe and effective for brain metastases in FAP-expressing advanced lung cancer, achieving intracranial tumor regression, symptom relief, and improved quality of life, thereby offering a promising therapeutic option for this refractory population.

item.title: [2.1] HER3 mediates metabolic reprogramming in metastatic colorectal and pancreatic cancer
item.description:
Liver metastases are a major cause of mortality in colorectal cancer (CRC) and pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC), yet the oncogenic signals that shape tumor metabolism in the hepatic niche remain poorly understood. Here, we show that HER3 activation drives a liver metastasis-specific glycolytic program in both cancer types. Genetic or pharmacological HER3 inhibition suppresses cancer glycolysis while increasing dependence on oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS), rendering liver metastases vulnerable to OXPHOS inhibition. Combining the HER3 inhibitor sapitinib with distinct OXPHOS inhibitors led to in vitro synergy and durable tumor-free survival in orthotopic CRC and PDAC liver metastases models, with further validation in patient-derived xenografts. Mechanistically, HER3 promotes glycolysis through activating PFK2 and reduces OXPHOS through activating DRP1-mediated mitochondrial remodeling, both pathways were activated in liver metastases compared to matched primary tumors. Together, our findings identify the HER3-AKT/RSK-PFK2 axis as a driver of glycolysis and metastatic growth and reveal an OXPHOS dependency induced by HER3 inhibition that may be exploited through combined HER3 and OXPHOS targeting in metastatic CRC and PDAC.

item.title: [1.6] SDHB deficiency silences ABCB1 expression and confers therapeutic vulnerability across multiple cancer types
item.description:
Succinate dehydrogenase B (SDHB)-deficient cancers, including pheochromocytoma and paraganglioma (PPGL), renal cell carcinoma (RCC), and gastrointestinal stromal tumor (GIST), exhibit aggressive clinical behavior with limited treatment options. To identify novel therapeutic vulnerabilities, we performed high-throughput drug screening using co-cultured human SDHB-deficient and SDHB-reconstituted UOK269 human renal cell carcinoma cells with dual fluorescence labeling. Several compounds displaying preferential cytotoxicity toward SDHB-deficient cells were known substrates of the ATP-binding cassette B1 (ABCB1) transporter, also known as Multidrug Resistance Protein 1 (MDR1). Accordingly, SDHB-deficient cells demonstrated markedly reduced ABCB1 expression, a phenotype confirmed across human SDHB-deficient PPGL, RCC, and GIST samples, but absent in IDH- or FH-deficient tumors. Mechanistic investigation revealed that KDM4A histone demethylase is downregulated in SDHB-deficient tumors, and KDM4A loss (or inhibition) is sufficient to reduce ABCB1 expression, globally increase H3K9me3 levels, and sensitize cells to cytotoxic ABCB1 substrates. TCGA analysis confirmed correlated KDM4A-ABCB1 expression in SDHB-deficient cancers, with ABCB1 levels predicting drug sensitivity across cancer cell lines. Clinical analysis demonstrated that SDHB-mutant PPGL patients treated with vincristine-containing chemotherapy exhibited significantly longer progression-free survival compared to non-SDHB patients. These findings establish a novel metabolic-epigenetic pathway linking SDHB deficiency to ABCB1 silencing and provide rational basis for repurposing vincristine, and related ABCB1 substrate vinca alkaloids, across SDHB-deficient cancer types; offering an alternative precision treatment approach for these challenging malignancies.

item.title: [2.9] Allele-Specific Mechanisms Guide Salvage Therapy to Overcome Daraxonrasib Resistance in Pancreatic Cancer
item.description:
Abstract Clinical-grade RAS inhibitors raise an unresolved question about whether KRAS alleles impose constraints on adaptive resistance that can be exploited therapeutically. Using daraxonrasib (RMC-6236), a multiselective RAS(ON) inhibitor, we compared resistance mechanisms between KRAS G12D and KRAS G12R , mutants with fundamentally different RAS network dynamics. Daraxonrasib inhibited mutant KRAS primarily through steric occlusion of effector binding while engaging wild-type RAS (RAS WT ) only modestly (∼20%). KRAS G12R was marked by its inability to transactivate RAS WT , and daraxonrasib-resistant KRAS G12R pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) cells utilized EGFR/RAS WT -GTP signaling as the dominant adaptive route. In contrast, KRAS G12D resistance arose through retained KRAS G12D -GTP signaling, with a decrease in cyclophilin A (CypA) protein, the binding partner required for daraxonrasib activity. The shift from KRAS G12R dependence to EGFR/RAS WT dependence conferred sensitivity to trametinib. As clinical confirmation, a patient with KRAS G12R PDAC who progressed after 10 months on daraxonrasib showed intratumoral EGFR/RAS WT activation, and rapid 3D-bioprinted patient-derived tumoroid modeling predicted sensitivity to trametinib-based combination therapy. Despite the aggressive disease trajectory and lack of response to the two immediately preceding lines of therapy, sixth-line trametinib-based combination therapy achieved approximately 5 months of disease control, and this patient ultimately achieved 40 months of overall survival, far exceeding the 8 to 12 months median for metastatic PDAC. Collectively, these data establish a framework in which allele-specific RAS network topology dictates the adaptive resistance landscape, enabling rational selection of targeted therapies with meaningful clinical benefit in metastatic PDAC. Significance: Daraxonrasib resistance emerges through allele-specific routes, with CypA being downregulated in KRAS G12D and reliance on EGFR/RAS WT in KRAS G12R cancer cells, informing mechanism-based therapeutic strategies for patients who progress on RAS inhibitors.
— Source: Cancer Research Current Issue

item.title: [2.2] Targeting GEM Reprograms Macrophages and Overcomes Immunotherapy Resistance in Esophageal Squamous Cell Carcinoma
item.description:
Abstract Esophageal squamous cell carcinoma (ESCC) exhibits heterogeneous responses to immune checkpoint blockade, highlighting the need to define tumor-intrinsic mechanisms driving resistance to PD-L1 inhibition. In this study, we identified GTP-binding protein overexpressed in skeletal muscle (GEM) as a tumor cell–intrinsic regulator associated with poor response to anti–PD-L1 therapy in ESCC. GEM expression in tumor cells drove tumor-associated macrophage–mediated immunosuppression, leading to reduced CD8 + T-cell infiltration and impaired cytotoxic function. Mechanistically, GEM induced serpin family E member 1 (SERPINE1) expression that was secreted and acted on macrophage low-density lipoprotein receptor–related protein 1 (LRP1) to drive alternative activation and suppress antitumor immunity. GEM enhanced SERPINE1 expression through a MKK3–RACK1–p38–MEF2A cascade. GEM signaling was reinforced by a metabolically coupled feedback mechanism. Macrophages exposed to GEM-high tumor cells promoted tumor cell glycolysis and lactate production, which drove AARS1-dependent lactylation of GEM and strengthened its interaction with RACK1 to amplify downstream signaling. Disruption of the SERPINE1–LRP1 axis restored CD8 + T-cell activity and enhanced response to PD-L1 blockade in vivo . Pharmacologic perturbation of GEM-dependent signaling remodeled the tumor immune microenvironment and improved responses to PD-L1 blockade. Together, these findings define a GEM–SERPINE1–LRP1 signaling axis that drives macrophage-mediated immunosuppression and suggest that targeting this pathway may enhance the efficacy of PD-L1 blockade in ESCC. Significance: GEM signaling engenders an immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment and promotes resistance to PD-L1 blockade, highlighting the potential of targeting GEM as a strategy to improve immunotherapy efficacy.
— Source: Cancer Research Current Issue

item.title: [1.7] Chronic Stress–Induced m 7 G Cap Modification of ADRB2 Dysregulates the Pentose Phosphate Pathway to Promote Esophageal Squamous Cell Carcinoma Progression
item.description:
Abstract Chronic stress is increasingly recognized as a driver of cancer metabolism, highlighting the need to elucidate the mechanism linking chronic stress to metabolic reprogramming. In this study, we performed untargeted metabolomics on serum samples from patients with esophageal squamous cell carcinoma (ESCC) and integrated the results with clinical and stress-related assessments, revealing pentose phosphate pathway (PPP) enrichment accompanied by elevated epinephrine levels in patients with stress-associated features. A β2-adrenergic receptor (ADRB2) activated by chronic stress stabilized MYC-binding protein (MYCBP) by competitively displacing VHL, thereby enhancing MYC transcriptional activity and upregulating key PPP enzymes, including G6PD and TKT. Unexpectedly, stress-associated stimulation not only activated ADRB2 signaling but also increased ADRB2 protein abundance. Mechanistically, stress exposure enhanced RNA guanine-7 methyltransferase (RNMT)-dependent N 7 -methylguanosine (m 7 G) cap modification of ADRB2 mRNA, thereby increasing its translational efficiency. Together, these findings define an RNMT–ADRB2–MYCBP–PPP axis that integrates epitranscriptomic regulation with adrenergic signaling to promote metabolic reprogramming and malignant progression in ESCC. The stress-associated RNA modification–metabolism circuitry comprises potential therapeutic targets to overcome stress-associated ESCC progression. Significance: Stress-associated signaling promotes esophageal squamous cell carcinoma progression through RNMT-dependent m 7 G cap modification of ADRB2 mRNA, enhancing adrenergic signaling, stabilizing MYCBP, and activating MYC-driven pentose phosphate pathway reprogramming.
— Source: Cancer Research Current Issue

item.title: [2.0] Phase Separation of ZBED2 Stabilizes ILK to Drive Metastasis and Immune Evasion in Esophageal Squamous Cell Carcinoma
item.description:
Abstract Metastasis remains a leading cause of mortality in patients with esophageal squamous cell carcinoma (ESCC), underscoring the urgent need to elucidate the molecular mechanisms driving disease progression. In this study, we delineated that zinc finger BED-type containing 2 (ZBED2), a zinc finger protein, correlates with inferior survival outcomes and metastasis in patients with ESCC. ZBED2 formed phase-separated nuclear condensates that functionally promote tumor metastasis, and integrin-linked kinase (ILK) was pinpointed as a critical downstream effector in mediating the prometastatic function of ZBED2. Mechanistically, ZBED2 enhanced the transcription of HSP90AA1, promoted the physical interaction between HSP90AA1 and ILK, and consequently stabilized ILK by suppressing its ubiquitination. Subsequently, ILK promoted PD-L1 transcription and CD8 + T-cell exhaustion, thereby creating an immunosuppressive microenvironment that facilitates cancer metastasis. Collectively, these findings establish the pivotal role of ZBED2 in driving ESCC metastasis and immune evasion, thereby validating it as a promising therapeutic target for this aggressive malignancy. Significance: A ZBED2-HSP90AA1-ILK-PD-L1 regulatory axis drives esophageal squamous cell carcinoma metastasis and immune evasion, identifying targeting ZBED2 as a potential therapeutic strategy for improving the prognosis of patients.
— Source: Cancer Research Current Issue

item.title: [1.7] Antibody–Drug Conjugates Synergize with Agonist Anti-CD137 Monoclonal Antibodies in Solid Tumors
item.description:
Abstract Antibody–drug conjugates (ADC) show clinical efficacy against several solid malignancies, inducing cytotoxic effects in malignant cells accompanied by changes in the composition of the tumor stroma. The therapeutic effects of some ADCs have been shown to be potentiated by combination with anti–PD-(L)1 checkpoint inhibitors, highlighting the potential of combining ADCs and immunotherapy. In this study, we investigated the potential of combining ADCs with agonist monoclonal antibodies targeting CD137 (4-1BB), a costimulatory receptor expressed on antigen-primed T lymphocytes and activated NK cells. The combination of monomethyl auristatin E– and deruxtecan-conjugated ADCs toward NECTIN-4 or HER2 with anti-CD137 agonists elicited synergistic effects in mouse tumor models. Treatment with the ADCs increased CD137 expression on intratumor CD8 + and CD4 + T lymphocytes. Moreover, the synergistic antitumor therapeutic efficacy was dependent on conventional type 1 dendritic cells (cDC1s) and CD8 + T cells. ADCs induced features of immunogenic cell death in malignant cells, resulting in cross-presentation and maturation of cDC1s that cross-prime CD8 + T cells to become CD137-positive. Importantly, the anti-CD137 plus ADC synergistic combination attained efficacy against concomitant tumor lesions that failed to express the ADC target. Together, these findings demonstrate that anti-CD137 agonists hold promise for combination strategies with ADCs. Significance: Antibody-drug conjugates synergize with CD137-agonists by inducing higher infiltration and surface expression of CD137 on CD8 + T cells as a result of cDC1-mediated cross-priming, eliciting robust antitumor activity.
— Source: Cancer Research Current Issue

item.title: [1.6] EphA4 Mediates Protumoral and Antitumoral Effects through Upstream Negative Regulation of AKT in Head and Neck Squamous Cell Carcinoma
item.description:
Abstract Head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC) is driven by an immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment (TME). We examined the immunomodulatory role of EphA4 in HNSCC using spatial analysis, multicompartment RNA sequencing from oral cavity squamous cell carcinoma, and three genetically engineered mouse models. Within the HNSCC TME, EphA4 is primarily expressed in regulatory T cells (Treg), macrophages, CD8 + T cells, and HNSCC cancer cells. EphA4 in Tregs promotes tumor growth, whereas EphA4 in myeloid cells, CD8 + T cells, and cancer cells limits it. EphA4 mediates these differential effects through shared negative regulation of AKT signaling where its knockout increases AKT activation, leading to reduced Treg immunosuppression, increased M2 macrophage polarization, impaired CD8 + T-cell memory differentiation, and enhanced cancer cell proliferation. APY-d3-PEG4, an EphA4 inhibitor, reduced tumor growth primarily by targeting Tregs. EphA4 expression on CD8 + T cells correlates with treatment response, representing a potential biomarker, and cell type–specific targeting via cis-bispecific antibodies offers a promising therapeutic strategy. Interrogating human data show that EphA4 expression on CD8 correlates to response to treatment, posing it as a potential biomarker for future studies. Mechanistically, our data show EphA4 inhibits AKT signaling, and its inhibition enhances AKT functionality across cell types, yielding opposing effects in cancer.
— Source: Cancer Immunology Research Current Issue

item.title: [1.7] Cancer Immunotherapy Using AIRE Conditioning of the Tumor Epitopeome
item.description:
Abstract T-cell immune tolerance is established in part through the activity of the autoimmune regulator (AIRE) transcription factor in medullary thymic epithelial cells (mTEC) of the thymus. AIRE induces expression of peripheral tissue–specific self-antigens for presentation to naïve T cells to promote activation/deletion of autoreactive T cells. This traditional role of AIRE in mTECs is to prevent autoimmunity. Herein, we demonstrate that tumors mimic the role of AIRE in mTECs to evade immune rejection. We found that AIRE induced a profile of “selfness” at the RNA and protein levels which, when presented on major histocompatibility complexes (MHC), shielded the tumor from inherently self-tolerized T cells. Moreover, we describe an in vivo immunotherapy in which engineered changes in AIRE expression in tumor cells altered their profile of selfness, exposing both AIRE-modified and parental unmodified tumor cells to T-cell attack. Therefore, by resetting the immunologic selfness of cancer cells, this AIRE-mediated immunotherapy (i) converted a highly tolerized T-cell compartment into a tumor-reactive T-cell population; (ii) conferred upon nonimmunogenic tumors de novo sensitivity to immune checkpoint blockade; (iii) removed the need to identify potentially immunogenic tumor-associated antigens as targets for generation of T-cell responses; and (iv) lead to potent T cell–mediated rejection of aggressive, immunologically cold, nonimmunogenic tumors. Patient RNA sequencing data showed that the expression of AIRE predicted response to immune therapies with a strong correlation between AIRE expression and markers of T-cell receptor signaling, suggesting that our studies have therapeutic translational value.
— Source: Cancer Immunology Research Current Issue

item.title: [2.0] The Posttranscriptional Regulator HuR Promotes Immune Evasion in Pancreatic Ductal Adenocarcinoma
item.description:
Abstract The tumor microenvironment (TME) of pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) is characterized by the restrained function of effector T cells that drive resistance to immunotherapy. Although tumor-extrinsic stroma and myeloid cells have been shown to mediate PDAC immune evasion, the role of tumor-intrinsic posttranscriptional gene regulation in driving tumor–immune cross-talk has been relatively unexplored. In this study, we report that the RNA-binding protein human antigen R (HuR; ELAVL1 ) is enriched in human PDAC and negatively correlates with T-cell infiltration. In two immunocompetent murine models of PDAC, we found that genetic disruption of HuR impaired tumor growth without significantly affecting in vivo proliferation. Comprehensive spatial and flow cytometry profiling of the PDAC TME revealed that genetic disruption of HuR in PDAC enhanced both T-cell number and functional state. Moreover, T-cell depletion abrogated the growth difference caused by HuR loss. Mechanistically, RNA immunoprecipitation sequencing, single-cell RNA sequencing, and orthogonal functional assays in vitro and in vivo showed that HuR stabilized mTOR pathway transcripts critical for metabolic adaptation in PDAC. HuR-driven metabolic reprogramming promoted tumor nutrient dominance and limited nutrient consumption by neighboring tumor-reactive T cells. Accordingly, HuR depletion sensitized PDAC tumors to immune checkpoint blockade and allowed for the expansion of tumor-specific T-cell populations, suggesting that HuR-mediated nutrient dominance and immune evasion have translational relevance. Overall, we found that the posttranscriptional regulator HuR facilitates immune evasion in PDAC by constraining T-cell function, identifying HuR blockade as a promising therapeutic strategy in combination with immunotherapies.
— Source: Cancer Immunology Research Current Issue

item.title: [1.6] Neutralizing the IL12/IL23 p40 Subunit Prevents Immune Checkpoint Blockade Toxicity without Compromising Antitumor Efficacy
item.description:
Abstract Immune checkpoint blockade (ICB) has markedly improved overall survival in various cancers but is associated with severe and sometimes fatal immune-related adverse events (irAE). Current management of irAEs involves discontinuation of ICB therapy and administration of immunosuppressive drugs, such as corticosteroids, which have been associated with decreased antitumor efficacy. Although irAE development is associated with ICB response, it is currently unknown whether their underlying mechanisms are shared or distinct. To identify early and targetable drivers of irAEs, we performed proteomic analyses on the serum of patients with cancer treated with anti–programmed cell death protein 1 (PD-1) and anti–cytotoxic T lymphocyte–associated protein 4 (CTLA-4) combination ICB. We identified a significantly increased concentration of p40, a subunit of interleukin (IL) 12/IL23, shortly after the start of ICB but before the onset of clinically apparent irAEs. Importantly, increased p40 levels were not associated with ICB efficacy. Neutralizing p40 mitigated ICB-induced toxicity in various mouse models without impairing ICB-induced antitumor efficacy. In conclusion, we demonstrated that IL12/IL23p40 is a key mediator of ICB-induced toxicity while being redundant for ICB antitumor efficacy. This shows that the mechanisms underlying ICB toxicity and efficacy can be uncoupled and provides a rationale for p40 blockade in clinical trials with ICB treatment to prevent irAEs in patients.
— Source: Cancer Immunology Research Current Issue

item.title: [1.9] Subtype-Agnostic Biomarkers of Immunotherapy Response in Lung Cancer
item.description:
Abstract Immunotherapy has transformed the lung cancer treatment landscape, establishing a role in nearly all histologic subtypes, including non–small cell and small cell lung cancers. However, only a few biomarkers, including PD-L1 tumor proportion score, tumor mutational burden, and microsatellite instability, are currently available, and their predictive value remains inconsistent across different histologies. The biological heterogeneity of lung tumors and the dynamic interplay between systemic therapies and the tumor microenvironment (TME) further complicate biomarker development. At the same time, novel immunotherapeutic strategies, including bispecific antibodies and antibody–drug conjugates, are expanding the spectrum of immune targets beyond conventional checkpoint inhibition, highlighting the need for biomarkers that better reflect the functional state of the TME. In this review, we address the limitations of currently used biomarkers across lung cancer histologies and describe emerging immune-related biomarkers encompassing innate immune infiltration, antigen presentation capacity, cytotoxic T-cell activation, and inflammatory signaling; these have shown promise as histology-independent predictors of response. Robust prospective studies are essential to validate integrated signatures capable of capturing profiles of patients who are most likely to respond to immune checkpoint inhibitors and next-generation treatments.
— Source: Cancer Immunology Research Current Issue

item.title: [1.8] Immune Checkpoint Blockade Sensitivity Is Linked to Endogenous Retroelement Transcriptional Changes in Cancer
item.description:
Abstract Endogenous retrotransposable elements (ERE) can modulate immune responses. We explored ERE transcription in relation to response to immune checkpoint inhibition in advanced solid tumors. ERE expression was measured in pre- and on-treatment samples from patients treated in a clinical trial with pembrolizumab. We evaluated immune cell infiltration and correlated ERE expression with interferon ( IFN )-stimulated gene profiles and cytolytic activity. Two independent datasets were retrospectively analyzed as external validation. ERE transcription, notably Alu repetitive elements followed by long interspersed nuclear elements (LINE), is upregulated in immunotherapy responders, and higher ERE expression correlates with durable clinical benefit and improved long-term outcomes. In responders, this dynamic increase correlates with CD8 + T-cell infiltration and cytolytic activity, particularly during treatment. A trend toward increased A-to-I RNA editing was observed in responders. External validation in melanoma and non–small cell lung cancer cohorts confirmed a consistent pattern in ERE transcription. Therefore, ERE transcription is emerging as a potential biomarker for personalized immunotherapy in solid tumors.
— Source: Cancer Immunology Research Current Issue

item.title: [1.8] COL1A1-Mediated BMP1–TGF-β Signaling Augments EMT and M2 Macrophage Polarization in Oral Squamous Cell Carcinoma
item.description:
Abstract Oral squamous cell carcinoma (OSCC) is a lethal malignancy characterized by frequent metastasis. Utilizing a 4-nitroquinoline 1-oxide–induced murine model and single-cell RNA sequencing, we identified a distinct collagen type I alpha 1 chain ( Col1a1 + ) epithelial subpopulation that is significantly expanded in OSCC, exhibits the highest epithelial–mesenchymal transition (EMT) signature, and correlates with poor patient survival. Functional studies demonstrated that Col1a1 knockdown (KD) in OSCC cell lines (HSC3, SCC25) attenuated transforming growth factor β (TGF-β)–induced EMT, impaired migration and invasion in vitro , and reduced tumor burden in a conditional knockout mouse model. Transcriptomic profiling following Col1a1 silencing revealed the suppression of TGF-β signaling and extracellular matrix (ECM)–receptor interaction pathways. We further identified BMP1 as a key downstream effector, demonstrating a direct physical interaction between COL1A1 and BMP1, and showed that COL1A1 potentiates BMP1’s proteolytic activity. Rescue experiments confirmed that BMP1 is essential for COL1A1-driven tumor growth, metastasis, and TGF-β pathway activation in vivo . Furthermore, we uncovered an immunomodulatory role for the COL1A1–BMP1 axis, whereby it promotes M2 macrophage polarization via TGF-β secretion to foster an immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment. This effect was reversible using either BMP1-KD or TGF-β neutralization. In conclusion, our study establishes a novel COL1A1–BMP1–TGF-β signaling cascade that drives OSCC progression by autonomously enhancing tumor cell malignancy and nonautonomously reprogramming the immune landscape, nominating this axis as a promising therapeutic target. Implications: These findings identify a novel COL1A1–BMP1 axis driving both OSCC malignancy and immunosuppression, offering potential diagnostic markers and therapeutic targets for the clinic.
— Source: Molecular Cancer Research Current Issue

item.title: [1.8] ADCE-T02: A Next-generation Antibody–Drug Conjugate Targeting Tissue Factor Demonstrates Superior Preclinical Efficacy and Tolerability
item.description:
Abstract Tissue factor (TF) protein is involved in activating the extrinsic blood coagulation cascade. TF expression is normally anatomically limited to the perivascular space, but TF is overexpressed in many malignancies, including pancreatic, cervical, prostate, and head and neck cancers, which makes TF an ideal antibody–drug conjugate (ADC) target. The TF-ADC tisotumab vedotin is approved for cervical cancer treatment but induces substantial side effects including ocular toxicities, peripheral neuropathy, and bleeding, limiting its further clinical development and warranting optimized ADC design to improve the therapeutic window. ADCE-T02 is a novel TF-ADC comprising the monoclonal antibody Ab-T02 conjugated via a self-immolative linker to the topoisomerase 1 inhibitor exatecan at an average drug-to-antibody ratio of 4.5. In contrast to tisotumab, Ab-T02 does not inhibit coagulation factor X activation. ADCE-T02 binds TF with high affinity inducing ADC internalization, exatecan release, cancer cell death, and bystander cytotoxicity in vitro . In vivo , ADCE-T02 is highly efficacious across a range of cell line–derived and patient-derived xenograft models including hard-to-treat models with large tumors, resistance to standard of care, low and/or heterogeneous expression of TF, and multidrug resistance. Importantly, ADCE-T02 demonstrates favorable pharmacokinetic properties and is well tolerated in nonhuman primates and in contrast to tisotumab vedotin and other auristatin-based ADCs shows no evidence of ocular, skin, and lung toxicities; peripheral nerve damage; or bleeding. In summary, ADCE-T02 constitutes a novel TF-ADC with a much improved preclinical therapeutic window. Phase I clinical development of ADCE-T02 in patients with advanced solid tumors is ongoing (ClinicalTrials ID: NCT06597721).
— Source: Molecular Cancer Therapeutics Current Issue

item.title: [1.7] Dual Inhibition of PARP and ATR Induces Synthetic Lethal Vulnerability in Prostate Cancer with CDK12 Deficiency
item.description:
Abstract Prostate cancers harboring CDK12 alterations exhibit aggressive clinical behavior and poor responses to current therapeutic strategies. Although CDK12 is categorized as a homologous recombination repair (HRR)–related gene, clinical evidence indicates limited benefit of poly (ADP-ribose) polymerase (PARP) inhibitor monotherapy in CDK12 -defective tumors. To clarify the functional consequences of CDK12 loss and identify a mechanistically rational therapeutic approach, we generated CDK12 -knockout (KO) prostate cancer cell lines using CRISPR/Cas9 and assessed cell-cycle regulation, DNA damage repair, and replication stress via flow cytometry, γH2AX immunofluorescence, and DNA fiber assays. CDK12 KO abrogated the G 0 –G 1 checkpoint, permitting cell-cycle progression into the M-phase despite the persistence of unrepaired DNA double-strand breaks (DSB), and reduced ATM transcription, resulting in a DSB response phenotype resembling ATM deficiency. CDK12 loss also increased intrinsic replication stress and sensitized prostate cancer cells to ATR inhibition. In patient-derived xenograft models harboring CDK12 alterations, combined PARP and ATR inhibition led to enhanced DSB accumulation and selectively suppressed tumor growth in CDK12 -defective models. These findings highlight the importance of interrogating individual genes within the HRR pathway to define distinct mechanistic vulnerabilities and provide a strong rationale for combined PARP and ATR inhibition as a novel therapeutic strategy for patients with CDK12 -altered prostate cancer.
— Source: Molecular Cancer Therapeutics Current Issue

item.title: [2.3] Suppression of AKT Activation through LZK Inhibition Limits Tumor Growth in Esophageal and Head and Neck Cancers
item.description:
Abstract Esophageal squamous cell carcinoma (ESCC) is one of the deadliest cancers worldwide due to its aggressive nature and lack of knowledge of underlying oncogenic drivers, limiting treatment options. Approximately 60% of ESCC cases have amplification/overexpression of MAP3K13 , which encodes the kinase LZK. In this study, we found that MAP3K13 -amplified ESCC exhibits therapeutic dependency on LZK and that small-molecule inhibition of its catalytic function decreased the viability of ESCC cells with amplified MAP3K13 . Inhibition of LZK suppressed tumor growth in MAP3K13 -amplified ESCC patient-derived xenograft mice treated orally with a newly described LZK inhibitor. We discovered that LZK is required to sustain AKT activation in ESCC and head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC), in which depletion, degradation, or treatment with the LZK inhibitor GNE-3511 or an improved inhibitor suppressed AKT activation. AKT activation could be rescued by the expression of an LZK drug-resistant mutant, indicating that suppression was specific to LZK. AKT and LZK co-localized and interacted in cells, and LZK enhanced AKT phosphorylation at S473 and T450 in vitro . This pattern of AKT phosphorylation reflected a noncatalytic scaffold function of LZK as LZK inhibitors did not suppress AKT activation and a kinase-dead LZK mutant promoted AKT activation. AKT inhibitors reduced LZK-induced activation of AKT, indicating that LZK facilitates AKT autophosphorylation. Furthermore, GNE-3511 inhibited the interaction of LZK with AKT in coimmunoprecipitation experiments. Molecular modeling supported a mechanism whereby LZK binds and dislodges AKT’s pleckstrin homology domain to promote AKT autophosphorylation. Our findings demonstrate that MAP3K13 -amplified tumors are dependent on LZK-mediated AKT scaffolding, supporting LZK inhibition as a therapeutic strategy in ESCC and HNSCC. Statement of significance: LZK promotes AKT autophosphorylation and tumor growth in ESCC and HNSCC; its inhibition suppresses AKT activation and viability, suggesting a novel therapeutic strategy for these cancers.
— Source: Molecular Cancer Therapeutics Current Issue

item.title: [1.8] Therapeutic Targeting of β-Catenin in Cancer
item.description:
Abstract Mutations in CTNNB1 (encoding β-catenin), together with recurrent genetic alterations affecting the WNT signaling pathway, define one of the most prevalent oncogenic axes, collectively occurring in approximately 10% of human cancers. Thus, β-catenin is a prime target for precision oncology. Over the three decades following the pathway’s discovery, substantial progress has been made in elucidating how aberrant WNT/β-catenin signaling can drive cancer initiation, progression, and maintenance. Attempts to therapeutically address this pathway have, until recently, been unsuccessful. Approaches to block the pathway upstream of relevant mutations were ineffective, whereas progress in directly targeting β-catenin, either by blocking its interaction with key complex partners, most notably T-cell factor proteins, or by inducing β-catenin degradation, has long remained an unreachable goal for conventional drug discovery approaches. In this review, we describe opportunities and challenges in the development of therapies that directly aim to target β-catenin. We highlight recent progress based on novel approaches, suggesting that cracking this previously considered “undruggable” central oncogenic driver is becoming a reality. Effective targeting of β-catenin has the potential to address extensive unmet patient needs in hard-to-treat cancer types such as colorectal cancer, hepatocellular carcinoma, and other cancers driven by WNT/β-catenin pathway alterations.
— Source: Molecular Cancer Therapeutics Current Issue

item.title: [1.8] QW-5-70 Targets the Colchicine Site and Demonstrates Antitumor Activity in P-gp–Overexpressing Cancer Models
item.description:
Abstract Drug resistance driven by efflux transporters and altered tubulin dynamics limits the clinical efficacy of taxanes and vincristine in high-risk neuroblastoma and castration-resistant prostate cancer. We developed QW-5-70, a colchicine binding site inhibitor (CBSI), engineered to retain low-nanomolar potency in both parental and drug-resistant cancer cells by showing minimal dependence on P-glycoprotein (P-gp)–mediated efflux. QW-5-70 binds to the colchicine site on tubulin, inhibits tubulin polymerization, disrupts microtubule networks, and induces mitotic arrest. Across a panel of neuroblastoma and prostate cancer lines, QW-5-70 maintained low-nanomolar activity and remained effective in vincristine-resistant BE2C/VCR and paclitaxel-resistant PC-3/TxR cells. Unlike vincristine and paclitaxel, the activity and intracellular accumulation of QW-5-70 were unaffected by pharmacologic or genetic inhibition of P-gp, indicating effective circumvention of efflux-mediated resistance. In vitro , QW-5-70 significantly reduced colony formation and impaired migration in both parental and resistant cancer cells and induced G 2 –M cell-cycle arrest and mitochondrial apoptosis. In vivo , QW-5-70 significantly suppressed tumor growth in drug-resistant PC-3/TxR and BE2C/VCR xenografts, with modest weight loss and no evident histopathology in the major organs. Combination studies revealed combination index–defined synergistic interactions at selected dose pairs with the ornithine decarboxylase inhibitor α-difluoromethylornithine and enhanced apoptotic and clonogenic suppression when combined with the Aurora A kinase inhibitor MLN8237. Collectively, QW-5-70 is a potent CBSI that circumvents P-gp–associated resistance, triggers mitotic arrest and apoptosis, and achieves significant antitumor activity in multidrug-resistant tumor models with acceptable tolerability, supporting its further preclinical development alone and in combination with other drugs.
— Source: Molecular Cancer Therapeutics Current Issue

item.title: [2.8] BLU-451, a CNS-Active, Potent, and Selective Small-Molecule Inhibitor against Uncommon EGFR Mutations
item.description:
Abstract BLU-451 is a potent and selective tyrosine kinase inhibitor designed to target uncommon epidermal growth factor receptor ( EGFR ) mutations, spare wild-type (WT) EGFR, and be active in the central nervous system (CNS). In vitro EGFR enzyme assays and engineered cell line models revealed selectivity and antiproliferative potency of BLU-451 against a wide range of EGFR mutations in non–small cell lung cancer, including common mutations, atypical mutations, and exon 20 insertions. Particularly, BLU-451 demonstrated robust antitumor activity in EGFR exon 20 insertion cell-derived and patient-derived xenograft models and was well tolerated in animal studies. Pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic analyses showed that BLU-451 suppressed exon 20 insertion phosphorylated EGFR expression levels within tumor tissues but not in skin and intestinal tissues, potentially indicative of lower toxicity associated with WT EGFR. In intracranial tumor models with imaging-based analyses, BLU-451 showed CNS antitumor efficacy. Early clinical data from patients enrolled in the phase I portion of the phase I/II CONCERTO trial (NCT05241873) demonstrated the overall clinical potential of BLU-451, including its CNS antitumor activity in patients with EGFR exon 20 insertions and atypical mutations. Initial data suggest that BLU-451 is an active molecule. Further evaluation of the safety profile and pharmacokinetic properties of BLU-451 is needed.
— Source: Molecular Cancer Therapeutics Current Issue

item.title: [2.5] Mechanisms of Acquired Resistance Following Dual EGFR/MET Inhibition in MET -Amplified EGFR TKI–Resistant Lung Cancer
item.description:
Abstract Mesenchymal–epithelial transition factor ( MET ) amplification is an epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) tyrosine kinase inhibitor (TKI) resistance mechanism that may be overcome by dual inhibition of EGFR and MET. However, acquired resistance after dual inhibition still occurs, and the mechanisms remain largely unknown. We analyzed resistance mechanisms after dual inhibition for MET amplification–mediated EGFR TKI resistance in lung cancer. Patient-derived cell lines were established before and after acquired resistance to dual inhibition, if possible. Potential resistance mechanisms were evaluated through signal pathway analysis and next-generation sequencing. Of 12 patients with resistance after EGFR/MET inhibition, 5 (42%) acquired oncogenic fusions (3 BRAF fusions, 1 ALK fusion, and 1 RET fusion), 1 (8%) developed EGFR T790M, 1 (8%) exhibited EGFR C797S, and 1 (8%) transformed to small cell. The EGFR T790M and ALK fusion responded to subsequent targeted therapies. Serial cell lines from a patient with EGFR L858R and MET amplification (PE5345), after resistance to osimertinib and capmatinib through gradual escalation of drug exposure in vitro (PE5345 os/cp R) and after clinical resistance to osimertinib and capmatinib (PE5867), were propagated. Novel acquired general transcription factor IIi– BRAF fusions emerged in PE5867. Osimertinib plus trametinib reversed resistance. PE5345 os/cp R overexpressed EGFR, which was inhibited by afatinib. Additionally, amivantamab induced significant antibody-dependent cell-mediated cytotoxicity (ADCC) against PE5345, PE5867, and PE5345 os/cp R. We found that resistance after dual inhibition is heterogeneous, but some might still be targetable. Amivantamab induced significant ADCC against both MET -amplified EGFR TKI-resistant cancer and resistant cells after dual EGFR/MET inhibition. Understanding resistance mechanisms may provide clues for subsequent therapy.
— Source: Molecular Cancer Therapeutics Current Issue

item.title: [1.6] Quantification of Antibody–Drug Conjugate Targets in Head and Neck Squamous Cell Carcinoma
item.description:
Abstract Antibody–drug conjugates (ADC) have shown clinical benefit in common solid tumors like breast cancer, lung cancer, and urothelial cancers but are just beginning to be investigated in head and neck cancer. We developed a quantitative immunofluorescence assay to reproducibly and accurately measure HER3 protein concentrations in formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded tissues. Using this assay, we measured HER3 protein concentrations in two head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC) tissue microarray cohorts containing 329 patients. Cell lines with mass spectrometry–measured protein concentrations were used to convert fluorescence signals to protein concentrations in amol/mm 2 . HER3, EGFR, and TROP2 showed a broad dynamic range in our cohorts with almost all of the cases above our assay’s limit of detection (LOD). Specifically, 100%, 97.5%, and 98.4% of cases have HER3, EGFR, and TROP2 levels above assay LOD. Interestingly, despite the previous demonstration of extremely low HER2 expression in HNSCC, 39.1% of cases showed HER2 expression above our assay LOD of 52.5 amol/mm 2 . When comparing between therapeutic targets, 97.2%, 99.3%, and 98.6% of cases are double-positive for HER3/EGFR, HER3/TROP2, and EGFR/TROP2, whereas only 34.2%, 34.6%, and 30.5% of cases are double-positive for HER3/HER2, EGFR/HER2, and TROP2/HER2. HER3, EGFR, and TROP2 are highly expressed in HNSCC. HER2 expression is relatively low in this HNSCC cohort compared with other ADC targets, but there are 39.1% of cases with detectable HER2 exceeding historic estimates. Overall, ADC target levels in HNSCC for approved ADCs suggest that patients with HNSCC may benefit from this class of drugs.
— Source: Molecular Cancer Therapeutics Current Issue

item.title: [1.7] H3K9me3 Regulates IFNγ low Tex Cell Differentiation to Promote Colon Tumor Liver Metastasis
item.description:
Abstract Despite the breakthrough in immune checkpoint inhibitor (ICI) immunotherapy in human cancer, colon cancer, except for the small subset of microsatellite instable human colon cancer, does not respond to ICI immunotherapy. As liver metastasis accounts for more than 90% of human colon cancer cases and mortality, ICI efficacy is primarily a measurement of liver metastasis suppression. Using a colon tumor liver metastasis syngeneic mouse model, we determined that mouse colon tumor liver metastases not only do not respond to anti–PD-1 immunotherapy but also exhibit no susceptibility to tumor-specific cytotoxic T lymphocyte (CTL) adoptive transfer immunotherapy. Analysis of human colon cancer liver metastases single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) datasets revealed that histone methyltransferases of histone 3 lysine 9 trimethylation (H3K9me3) are upregulated in colon tumors and expressed in subsets of T cells in liver metastases of patients with human colon cancer. Targeted therapy with the H3K9me3-specific histone methyltransferase inhibitor F5446 suppresses colon tumor liver metastasis. scRNA-seq analysis revealed the accumulation of PD-1 + Tim3 + exhausted T (Tex) cells in mouse colon tumor liver metastases, and F5446 treatment increased the level of IFNγ high PD-1 low Tex cells. Furthermore, F5446 therapy increased IFNγ high intermediate Tex (Tex-int) cells in human colon cancer patient liver metastases–derived xenografts (PDX) and suppressed PDX growth in humanized mice. In patients with human colon cancer, response to pembrolizumab is associated with tumor-infiltrating IFNγ high Tex cells. Our findings determine that H3K9me3 promotes differentiation of Tex cells and targeting H3K9me3 is an effective approach to increase IFNγ high Tex-int cells to reinvigorate CTL functionality to suppress colon cancer liver metastasis.
— Source: Molecular Cancer Therapeutics Current Issue

item.title: [1.6] Potent Anti-Tumor Activity of the AXL-Targeted Antibody-Drug Conjugate, Mipasetamab Uzoptirine (ADCT-601), in Preclinical Models of Adenoid Cystic Carcinoma
item.description:
Abstract Adenoid cystic carcinoma (ACC) is a rare salivary gland malignancy with no FDA-approved systemic therapies and limited benefit from conventional treatments. Proteogenomic profiling has revealed consistent overexpression of AXL, providing a compelling rationale to pursue AXL as a novel therapeutic target. We investigated mipasetamab uzoptirine (ADCT-601), an AXL-targeting antibody-drug conjugate (ADC) with pyrrolobenzodiazepine dimer payload, in preclinical models of ACC. In vitro cytotoxicity was assessed in AXL-positive cell lines, and in vivo efficacy was evaluated using cell line xenograft and patient-derived xenograft (PDX) models. ADCT-601 demonstrated potent and selective cytotoxicity in AXL-expressing ACC cell lines. In xenograft models, a single administration at 0.5 or 1.0 mg/kg induced significant tumor regression, with complete tumor eradication observed at 1.0 mg/kg. Across a panel of ACC PDX models, ADCT-601 produced strong yet variable anti-tumor activity, with therapeutic response correlating with AXL expression levels. ADCT-601 demonstrates robust AXL expression linked to anti-tumor activity in preclinical models of ACC, establishing a proof of concept for targeting AXL in this rare cancer. These findings support clinical translation of AXL-targeting ADC as a novel biomarker-driven therapy for patients with ACC.
— Source: Molecular Cancer Therapeutics Current Issue

item.title: [1.7] APR-246 and DNA polymerase theta inhibitor Novobiocinsynergize to eliminate TP53 mutant AML cells
item.description:
Patients with TP53-mutant myelodysplasic syndromes (MDS) and acute myeloid leukemia (AML) are usually elderly and frail with highly resistant malignant clones and a median survival of less than one year. The molecule APR-246 targets mutant p53 but also perturbs redox homeostasis. APR-246 showed favorable safety in a phase 3 trial in TP53 mutant MDS/AML but did not meet efficacy endpoints in combination with azacitidine (AZA), highlighting the need for more effective combination strategies. Conversion of APR-246 to the active compound MQ releases formaldehyde which generates DNA-protein crosslinks. AML cells depend on DNA polymerase theta (Pol[O]) to repair such lesions and Pol[O] protects cells from ferroptosis. Using a panel of isogenic MOLM13 AML cell lines each carrying a common TP53 variant, we show that the Pol[O] inhibitor Novobiocin (NVB) synergizes with APR-246 to induce AML cell death. We demonstrate strong synergy with this combination in all TP53 mutant cell lines and to a lesser extent in the TP53 wildtype and null cells, indicating both p53-dependent and p53-independent mechanisms behind the synergy. APR-246 provides selectivity for TP53-mutated cells while NVB enhances p53-independent apoptosis and p53-dependent ferroptosis. Levels of ferroptosis induction correlate with the observed synergy in TP53-mutant and WT cells. Combination of APR-246 and NVB induces potent in vitro growth inhibition of primary TP53-mutated AML/CMML patient samples, with significant activity achieved at low micromolar or nanomolar concentrations of APR-246. Our findings hold promise for combination of APR-246 and NVB as a new therapeutic strategy tailored for TP53-mutated AML patients with high efficacy and low toxicity.

item.title: [2.8] Targeting KRAS Codon 13 Mutations Using Direct Combination Approaches in Non–Small Cell Lung Cancer
item.description:
Abstract Direct inhibitors of KRAS G12C are now used as standard-of-care therapy in KRAS G12C -mutant non–small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), but less is understood about the molecular mechanisms and consequent treatment vulnerabilities of KRAS codon 13 mutations in this setting. In this study, we characterized the tumorigenic properties of NSCLC harboring KRAS G13X in a large multinational cohort of patients with NSCLC and in preclinical models of KRAS G13X NSCLC. Induction of KRAS G13C or KRAS G13D expression confers reduced oncopotency compared with allele-specific controls affecting KRAS codon 12, particularly KRAS G13C . We identified functionally relevant comutations in KRAS G13X NSCLC, including KEAP1 , STK11 , BRAF , and NF1 . The novel RAS(ON) G13C-selective inhibitor, RMC-8839, reduces viability in a panel of KRAS G13C NSCLC cell models. To determine combination partners that enhance RAS(ON) mutant-selective inhibition, a drug repurposing screen revealed that KRAS G13C models are selectively vulnerable to chemotherapy. Combination of docetaxel with RMC-8839 demonstrated robust antiproliferative activity in KRAS G13C -driven NSCLC models in vitro and in vivo . Significance: We characterize the second most common KRAS mutational hotspot in NSCLC after codon 12, KRAS G13X , from tumor initiation to advanced disease. KRAS G13C is a novel, directly targetable subset of NSCLC, with vulnerability to the combination of chemotherapeutics and the mutant-selective RAS(ON) inhibitor RMC-8839, a finding immediately relevant to patient care. See related commentary by Araujo and Skoulidi, p. 2206 See related article by Seamon et al., p. 2256
— Source: Cancer Discovery Current Issue

item.title: [2.7] EML4−ALK Mediates Resistance to KRAS G12C Inhibition and Induces an Oncogenic Dependency by Rewiring Signaling through the Wild-Type RAS Pathway
item.description:
Abstract KRAS mutations are common oncogenic drivers in human cancers, with the KRAS G12C variant being a key target in lung adenocarcinoma. Despite the FDA approval of KRAS G12C -selective inhibitors, their clinical efficacy has been limited, as evidenced by trials showing modest response rates and resistance development through the selection of acquired genomic alterations. Our study explores the mechanisms underlying acquired EML4–ALK fusion in KRAS G12C -driven tumors developing resistance to KRAS G12C inhibitors and potential therapeutic strategies to overcome it. Our findings reveal that combined ALK/KRAS G12C inhibition is an effective therapeutic approach in this context. Moreover, we observed that KRAS G12C /EML4–ALK tumor cells kept under constant pressure with KRAS G12C inhibitors exhibit sensitivity to single-agent ALK inhibitors, suggesting a potential for rationally designed sequential treatments. Mechanistically, EML4–ALK bypasses KRAS G12C inhibition by activating wild-type RAS, highlighting an additional therapeutic opportunity for multiselective RAS inhibitors under clinical investigation. Significance: Acquired EML4–ALK fusions confer resistance to KRAS inhibition in KRAS G12C -driven lung adenocarcinoma. By rewiring the oncogenic signaling under inhibitor pressure, EML4–ALK creates a new oncogenic dependency that can be exploited for more effective therapeutic strategies. See related commentary by Araujo and Skoulidi, p. 2206
— Source: Cancer Discovery Current Issue

item.title: [1.6] CDK8 Inhibition Induces Mediator Trapping and Impairment of the EWSR1::FLI1 Transcriptional Program in Ewing Sarcoma
item.description:
Abstract Ewing sarcoma is characterized by a chromosomal translocation resulting in the fusion protein EWSR1::FLI1. We utilize endogenous EWSR1::FLI1 target gene reporters in patient-derived cell lines to perform a high-throughput phenotypic screen to identify small molecules that impair the EWSR1::FLI1 transcriptional program. We discovered that inhibitors of cyclin-dependent kinase 8 (CDK8), including a novel pyridyl imidazole, altered transcription of EWSR1::FLI1 target genes and CDK8 co-localized with EWSR1::FLI1 preferentially on single GGAA DNA-binding motifs. Using pooled CRISPR screening, biochemical studies, and chromatin profiling, we discovered that CDK8 inhibitors suppressed proliferation of Ewing sarcoma cells through a gain-of-function mechanism by inducing molecular trapping of the CDK8 kinase module and Mediator complex on chromatin. This mechanism has implications for the development of small molecules to target transcription and suggests that impairment of transcriptional regulatory complex dynamics might serve as a vulnerability in cancers in which the dominant oncogenes act as dosage-sensitive transcription factors. Significance: A high-throughput screen using endogenous EF target gene reporter alleles identified CDK8 as a modifier of EF transcriptional regulation. Using pooled CRISPR screening, biochemical studies, and chromatin profiling, we discovered that CDK8 inhibitors impaired transcriptional regulation through molecular trapping of CDK8 and the Mediator complex on chromatin. See related commentary by Stevens and Hatley, p. 2210

item.title: [1.9] Serpins Establish Fibrin-Rich Suppressive Niches in Pancreatic Cancer
item.description:
Major Finding: Serpins drive fibrin-dependent immune suppression and resistance to PD-1 blockade. Concept: Tumor-derived serpins locally reshape the extracellular matrix and promote macrophage polarization to suppress immune surveillance. Impact: Targeting the serpin–fibrin axis may enhance immunotherapy by reducing suppressive macrophages and promoting CD8 + T-cell infiltration.

item.title: [2.7] Selective Inhibition of KRAS G13C Reveals an Increased Dependence on Wild-type RAS Isoforms in Codon 13 RAS-Mutant Cancers
item.description:
Abstract Covalent KRAS G12C inhibitors have changed the treatment landscape for patients with non–small cell lung cancer and colorectal cancer, but numerous RAS-mutant cancers lack approved targeted therapies. In this study, we describe RMC-8839, an oral RAS(ON) G13C-selective, covalent, tricomplex inhibitor that induced tumor regressions in selected KRAS G13C -mutant xenograft models. However, one third of KRAS G13C -mutant human cancer cell lines in vitro showed incomplete RAS pathway suppression despite near-complete KRAS G13C engagement, suggesting a role for wild-type RAS(ON). We find that codon 13–mutant RAS differs from other KRAS mutations, exhibiting decreased stability, increased nucleotide exchange, and substantial intrinsic and guanosine triphosphatase-activating protein–stimulated GTP hydrolysis, which decreases oncogenicity. Furthermore, co-occurring RAS pathway mutations leading to increased wild-type RAS activation are enriched in codon 13–mutant tumors. Consistent with a role for wild-type RAS(ON) signaling, the combination of RMC-8839 with a RAS(ON) multiselective inhibitor resulted in deeper inhibition of KRAS G13C -mutant xenograft tumor growth than either inhibitor alone. Significance: An enhanced understanding of the underlying biology of RAS mutations is critical to inform therapeutic strategies. Our preclinical data highlight that codon 13 mutant tumors are more reliant on wild-type RAS signaling than codon 12 tumors and demonstrate that this can be addressed by combining RAS(ON) G13C-selective and multiselective inhibitors. See related commentary by Araujo and Skoulidi, p. 2206 See related article by McDaid et al., p. 2274
— Source: Cancer Discovery Current Issue

item.title: [1.6] Tumor-Derived Antioxidants Suppress T-Cell Activation
item.description:
Major Finding: Tumor-derived antioxidants disrupt reactive oxygen species (ROS) balance within the tumor microenvironment, suppressing antitumor immunity. Concept: Peroxiredoxin 1 (PRDX1)-mediated ROS depletion inhibits signaling and effector function of T cells. Impact: PRDX1-driven tumor immunosuppression highlights redox state as a potential targetable vulnerability.
— Source: Cancer Discovery Current Issue

item.title: [2.0] Macropinocytosis Enables Recyclable Lysosome-Targeting Chimeras
item.description:
Major Finding: A receptor-independent lysosome-targeting chimera (LYTAC) shuttles its target to the lysosome for degradation and recycles to the cell surface. Concept: A zwitterionic polymer drives uptake by macropinocytosis, and vesicle acidification releases the target, letting the degrader escape via exocytosis. Impact: Receptor-independent recycling widens targeted protein degradation to tumors lacking expression of recycling receptors and enhances the degradation efficiency.
— Source: Cancer Discovery Current Issue

item.title: [2.2] Phase III Trials Test First-Line Options in Advanced NSCLC
item.description:
Abstract: Presented at the 2026 World Conference on Lung Cancer, two phase III trials—PAPILLON and REZILIENT3—established amivantamab and zipalertinib combination therapies as effective first-line strategies for advanced NSCLC with EGFR exon 20 insertions, with significantly improved progression-free survival, although high crossover rates prevented them demonstrating an overall survival benefit. Separately, HARMONi-2 showed that the bispecific antibody ivonescimab improved overall survival versus pembrolizumab in PD-L1–positive NSCLC, supporting its use as standard of care in China while larger global trials continue.
— Source: Cancer Discovery Current Issue

item.title: [1.7] Lymphoid Structures within Skull Bone Marrow Promote Immunosurveillance
item.description:
Main Finding: Skull bone marrow contains germinal center-like niches that mount early antigen-specific responses to brain tumors. Concept: T FH cells and B cells in skull bone marrow support local immunosurveillance of brain-derived antigens. Impact: Boosting the lymphoid response of skull bone marrow may enhance antitumor immunity in brain cancers.
— Source: Cancer Discovery Current Issue

item.title: [2.0] A Pan-Cancer Single-Cell Analysis of Intratumoral Copy-Number Diversity and Evolution
item.description:
Abstract Aneuploidy is a hallmark of human tumors. Although patient-level copy-number alteration (CNA) differences have been investigated extensively in large cohorts, their intratumoral heterogeneity remains understudied. In this study, we conducted a pan-cancer analysis of 94 human tumors at single-cell resolution, representing seven cancer types: bladder, breast, colon, glioblastoma, kidney, lung, and ovarian. Single-cell copy-number profiling was used to analyze 62,646 aneuploid cells, in addition to bulk exome sequencing of most patients and single-nucleus RNA sequencing of six samples. In many cancer types, increased subclonal diversity was associated with higher CNA burden, whole-genome doubling (WGD), TP53 mutations, and increased geographic diversity. Cancer cells from each patient shared a set of truncal CNAs, suggesting evolution from a single ancestral cell. Many tumors accumulated CNAs in bursts of evolution, suggesting that punctuated evolution is common in diverse cancer types. This study greatly improves our knowledge of intratumoral chromosome diversity across human cancers. Significance: This study presents one of the largest pan-cancer single-cell DNA sequencing analyses, profiling intratumoral copy-number heterogeneity across seven major cancer types. The data identified punctuated evolution, clonal origins, subclonal WGD, spatial heterogeneity, and associations between copy-number and transcriptional diversity, with implications for both cancer diagnosis and treatment.
— Source: Cancer Discovery Current Issue

item.title: [2.8] Expanding the RAS-verse: Novel Inhibitors, Emergent Dependencies, Fresh Opportunities in RAS -Mutant NSCLC
item.description:
Summary: In this issue, two studies establish KRAS G13C as a directly targetable oncoprotein in non–small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) while revealing distinct dependence of codon 13–mutant NSCLC on wild-type (WT) RAS and enhanced sensitivity to standard-of-care chemotherapy. A third study highlights rewired oncogenic signaling through WT RAS as a therapeutically tractable mechanism of resistance to KRAS G12C inhibitors in the context of acquired oncogenic kinase fusions. item.title: [1.8] It’s a Trap! CDK8 Inhibition Reveals a Shared Vulnerability through Mediator Trapping in Fusion-Driven Pediatric Sarcomas
item.description:
Summary: A large proportion of pediatric sarcomas are driven by neomorphic transcription factors that are challenging therapeutic targets. In this issue, two independent studies identify CDK8 as a shared therapeutic vulnerability in pediatric fusion oncoprotein–driven sarcomas and reveal that CDK8 inhibitors disrupt oncogenic transcriptional programs through an unexpected gain-of-function mechanism involving Mediator complex trapping on chromatin. item.title: [2.4] Targeting RAS for Pancreatic Cancer Interception
item.description:
Summary: Multiple strategies to target RAS are now available to treat pancreatic cancer. As pancreatic precancers also have KRAS mutations, these tools hold great promise for cancer interception.

item.title: [1.7] New Studies Showcase Capabilities of Organoids
item.description:
Abstract: Three recent papers show the potential benefits of several hundred new organoids, spheroids, and other cancer models. One study demonstrates that more than 600 of the models mirror their parent tumors. A second study uses organoids to uncover new cancer dependencies, or essential genes, in 147 organoids from 10 cancer types. The third study also identifies new cancer dependencies and shows that organoids from individual patients might lead to new treatment choices.
— Source: Cancer Discovery Current Issue

item.title: [1.7] Q&A: Eileen O’Reilly on Pancreatic Cancer
item.description:

O’Reilly, MD, a medical oncologist at Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center in New York, NY, whose research focuses on therapies for pancreas cancer, spoke with Cancer Discovery ’s Suzanne Rose about daraxonrasib combinations, treatment strategies under development, the need for genomic testing, and what big headlines might come in pancreas cancer.
