item.title: [1.9] Spatial Proximity Mapping Identifies Vulnerabilities for Therapeutic Co-Targeting
item.description:
Major Finding: Proximity mapping identifies CDCP1 as a tumor-associated proximity antigen partner of EGFR, wherein co-targeting of EGFR and CDCP1 boosts tumor cell killing across multiple modalities. Concept: Photocatalytic proximity labeling and graph-based machine learning map tumor surface protein networks. Impact : The concept of tumor-associated proximity antigens is a promising tool to identify novel and tumor-specific therapeutic co-targets.
— Source: Cancer Discovery Current Issue

item.title: [1.9] Nucleoporins in Cancer: Functional Roles and Therapeutic Opportunities
item.description:
Abstract The nuclear pore complex (NPC) and its building-block proteins, nucleoporins (NUP), play fundamental roles in maintaining cellular fitness by regulating nucleocytoplasmic transport, chromatin and transcriptional activity, and genome stability. These core biological processes are critical for cancer cells, and thus, tumor-driven co-option of NUP-regulated functions has emerged as an important mechanism contributing to the pathogenesis of multiple malignancies. This review discusses how NUP dysregulation mechanistically contributes to tumor initiation and progression and how these insights open opportunities for innovative anticancer therapies, including using clinical-grade molecular glues that induce selective NUP degradation and pharmacologically inhibiting NPC-regulated epigenomic/transcriptomic signaling and nucleocytoplasmic transport. Significance: Recent studies demonstrate that NUPs play fundamental roles in cancer pathogenesis by dysregulating key NPC functions and driving tumorigenesis and disease progression. NUPs and NPC-regulated mechanisms can be pharmacologically targeted, providing a strong rationale for developing much-needed innovative therapeutic strategies to combat cancer.
— Source: Cancer Discovery Current Issue

item.title: [1.9] Binding-To-Release Enhances Efficacy of Small Molecule–Drug Conjugates
item.description:
Major Finding: Binding-to-release (BTR) drug conjugates inhibit tumor growth in multiple tumor models by specifically and efficiently delivering a membrane-permeable cytotoxic payload. Concept: PhoPEx-based conjugates can be cleaved upon extracellular target binding, eliminating the need for endocytosis-mediated payload release. Impact: This study provides a framework for an innovative therapeutic strategy that can be generalized for various target proteins and tumor types.
— Source: Cancer Discovery Current Issue

item.title: [1.5] Revamped transposon-induced hepatocellular carcinoma model reveals deep similarities of cancer-driver landscapes across mice and humans
item.description:
Genome-scale cancer-driver discovery is limited by statistical uncertainty in driver calling and by experimental constraints on mutations available for selection. We developed 3xfOnc3 - a three-frame Sleeping Beauty (SB) mutagenesis system designed to broaden functional perturbations and reduce integration biases of traditional SB screens - and tested it in vivo in mouse liver. Within 12 months, 60% of mice developed heterogeneous hepatocellular tumors. Tumor-selected integrations were interpreted against an empirical reference from SB-based therapeutic gene delivery to hepatocytes, enabling correction for gene targetability. Background-aware filtering prioritized 315 driver candidates, including 243 protein-coding genes. Tumors were multiclonal, and identical integration-marked lineages expanded differently across lesions, supporting context-dependent clonal expansion. SB hits within young L1 subfamily members were selectively enriched in tumors. Human orthologues of candidate drivers were enriched for Cancer Gene Census genes and protein-altering pan-cancer mutations. Together, 3xfOnc3 reveals a background-corrected driver landscape linking driver selection to clonal tumor evolution and cross-species cancer relevance.

item.title: [1.6] Aneuploidy profiling among different types of brain metastases reveals a colon cancer-specific chromosomal signature
item.description:
Brain metastasis is a significant cause of patient morbidity and mortality. There is increasing evidence that genomic instability features such as aneuploidy are associated with metastases to the brain and other organs. We analyzed the genomic instability of brain metastases among different cancer types. This included brain metastases from non-small cell lung, breast, melanoma and colorectal cancer. Our study identified a significantly higher degree of genomic instability in colorectal brain metastases compared to the other types of brain metastases. Nex, we examined the brain metastases for the types of aneuploidy events, namely chromosomal arm imbalances that involved gains or losses. Colorectal cancer brain metastases had specific chromosomal arm imbalance profiles that included gains of 13q and 20q which were significantly more frequent compared to the other cancer types. We examined other colorectal cancer metastatic sites in the lung, liver, lymph nodes and the primary colon. Examining colorectal cancer metastases more closely, aneuploidy gains across either arms for chromosomes 7 and 16 were also higher among brain metastases compared to liver, lung and lymph node metastases. Overall, this study shows that colorectal cancer brain metastasis has specific aneuploidy profiles different than other cancer types as well as being different among other metastatic organ sites.
— Source: bioRxiv Subject Collection: Cancer Biology

item.title: [1.9] Mapping chromothripsis across human cancer cell lines reveals genome evolution and therapeutic vulnerabilities
item.description:
Chromothripsis is a catastrophic chromosomal rearrangement found in ~40% of primary tumors, yet its landscape in cancer cell lines (CCLs) remains uncharacterized. To address this gap, we developed a pipeline to detect chromothripsis-like events from copy-number data alone, and mapped their occurrence across 1,646 human CCLs. Chromothripsis patterns were broadly conserved between primary tumors and CCLs, but CCLs displayed some distinct features and a significantly higher prevalence of chromothripsis. Chromothripsis continued to emerge during culture propagation, likely contributing to its increased prevalence in CCLs. Integrating genomic and functional data revealed selective vulnerabilities: chromothriptic cells were resistant to DNA damage-inducing agents but highly sensitive to histone deacetylase inhibitors (HDACi). Using isogenic models, we validated that HDACi could synergistically sensitize chromothriptic cells to DNA damage-inducing agents. Our study establishes the first comprehensive resource of chromothripsis in CCLs and reveals functional consequences and therapeutic vulnerabilities of chromothripsis-positive cancers.
— Source: bioRxiv Subject Collection: Cancer Biology

item.title: [2.0] Neuro-mimetic reprogramming and epigenetic unlocking drive lung cancer stem cell adaptation to the brain microenvironment
item.description:
Brain metastasis represents a lethal complication of non-small cell lung cancer, driven by the ability of disseminated tumor cells to colonize the central nervous system microenvironment. Although cancer stem cells (CSCs) are recognized as key drivers of metastatic initiation, whether their contact with the brain parenchyma induces terminal differentiation or adaptive plasticity remains controversial. Here, using an in vivo model of lung-derived CSCs injected intracranially, combined with quantitative total proteomics and phosphoproteomics, we demonstrate that contact with the brain niche triggers a neuro-mimetic reprogramming rather than terminal differentiation. Lung CSCs desensitize their systemic metastatic program while epigenetically unlocking neural stem cell networks, characterized by the upregulation of Ngfr, Fabp7, Pbx3, Vgf, and S100b, concurrent with the downregulation of the DNA methyltransferase Dnmt3a and the cytosolic exclusion of Id1. Phosphoproteomic profiling revealed post-translational adaptations, highlighted by hyperphosphorylation of Nestin at S957 and S963. Furthermore, kinase substrate enrichment analysis uncovered high activity of Prkcq (PKC{theta}) and Map3k7 (TAK1), shifting the cellular state toward structural remodelling and microenvironmental stress tolerance. Functional validation assays using selective inhibitors confirmed that these kinase networks represent adaptive liabilities within tissue constraints rather than basic in vitro survival requirements. Together, our findings demonstrate that lung CSCs exploit a phenotypic plasticity to adapt to the brain niche, acquiring a neural-glial disguise that supports vascular co-option, immune evasion, and metastatic colonization.
— Source: bioRxiv Subject Collection: Cancer Biology

item.title: [1.5] Gene context shapes spatial organization and transcriptional heterogeneity of extrachromosomal DNA in cancer cells
item.description:
Extrachromosomal DNA (ecDNA) promotes tumor adaptability by making oncogenic driver genes variably abundant, spatially mobile, and heterogeneously expressed. Transcriptional hyperactivation and spatial mobility of ecDNA-amplified genes is associated with aberrant regulatory states that could create targetable vulnerabilities in ecDNA-driven cancers. However, how gene context shapes their nuclear positioning and aberrant transcription remains unclear. To explore spatio-transcriptional behavior across ecDNA-amplified genes, we developed FLAGx, a multimodal imaging method that quantitatively resolves transcriptional activity and nuclear position of individual ecDNA genes in situ. Surprisingly, we find that gene context affects subnuclear distribution and transcriptional deregulation of ecDNA. Further, ecDNA clustering, cell cycle regulation, and drug responses depend on gene context, while transcriptional shutdown in mitosis persists across ecDNA species, arguing against pervasive mitotic transcription as a common feature. These findings show that driver gene context shapes ecDNA behavior and establish FLAGx as a useful approach to separate gene-specific from shared ecDNA features.

item.title: [1.6] A CTCF-LDHB axis converts nuclear lactate availability into an H3K18 acylation switch that directs alternative splicing in hypoxic breast cancer
item.description:
Lactate accumulating in hypoxic tumours lactylates histones, coupling metabolic state to chromatin. Why it differs between tumours of comparable glycolytic rate has remained unresolved. Here we show that nuclear, rather than total intracellular, lactate availability determines histone H3K18 lactylation in breast cancer, and that CCCTC-binding factor (CTCF) and lactate dehydrogenase B (LDHB) jointly set it. CTCF sustains glycolytic gene expression under hypoxia and drives LDHB in triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC), whereas a CTCF-ER complex represses LDHB in non-TNBC. LDHB consumes lactate favouring H3K18 acetylation; where LDHB is low, CTCF-dependent MCT1 delivers lactate into the nucleus and sustains lactylation. At a CTCF site downstream of TACC3 exon 3, an invariant polymerase II pause couples kinetic and adaptor control of splicing, with the mark deciding the outcome: H3K18la recruits SMARCA4 and hnRNPA1 to skip the exon, generating an isoform that drives EMT, whereas H3K18ac recruits TRIM33 and SRSF10 to include it, generating one that confers stemness. Inhibiting LDHB restores exon skipping and suppresses tumour growth in vivo. Nuclear lactate availability therefore acts as a metabolic switch that converts hypoxic stress into subtype-specific splicing decisions and identifies LDHB as a tractable target in TNBC.
— Source: bioRxiv Subject Collection: Cancer Biology

item.title: [2.3] Activated ADAM10 targeting antibody 1H5 suppresses NOTCH-driven glioma progenitors
item.description:
Background: High-grade gliomas (HGGs) remain associated with high morbidity, mortality, and invariable recurrence after neurosurgical resection and chemoradiation. A major contributor to treatment failure is a population of stem-like glioma progenitor cells (GPCs) that depend on NOTCH-signaling for self-renewal and survival; clinical attempts to inhibit NOTCH with {gamma}-secretase inhibitors failed due to systemic toxicity. Methods: Here, we investigate the anti-HGG therapeutic potential of a fully-human monoclonal antibody, 1H5, that selectively targets activated-ADAM10, an -secretase required for NOTCH receptor processing, with high tumor specificity. We show that ADAM10 is markedly overexpressed and highly activated in primary and recurrent HGGs, using patient tissue, RNA-sequencing data, and early-passage HGG cell lines. Results: Across a panel of patient-derived HGG lines, sensitivity to 1H5 correlates with the cell-surface levels of activated-ADAM10, and shRNA-mediated ADAM10 knockdown recapitulates the growth-inhibitory effects of 1H5. ADAM10 inhibition suppresses NOTCH-pathway components and target genes, reduces expression of GPC markers, and impairs neurosphere formation while depleting Sox2- and Ki67-positive cells. We further find that 1H5 induces HGG cell death predominantly via necroptosis, characterized by survivin loss and increased phosphorylated MLKL and by transcriptional changes in necroptosis-related genes. In three-dimensional explants derived from primary HGG, 1H5 reduces growth and GPC marker expression while increasing TUNEL staining. Finally, convection-enhanced delivery of 1H5 in orthotopic xenograft models achieves high local intracranial concentrations, slows tumor growth, and prolongs survival, with regional pharmacodynamic effects consistent with NOTCH pathway suppression and necroptosis.

item.title: [2.4] Glioblastoma Hijacks Astrocyte Ribosomes to Feul Malignancy through Translatome Reprogramming
item.description:
Cancer cells demand elevated protein synthesis, yet whether they directly requisition ribosomes from microenvironmental host cells remains unknown. Here, utilizing in vivo and in vitro ribosome tracing, we show that glioblastoma (GBM) cells hijack ribosomes from surrounding astrocytes via tunneling nanotube-like structures. This transfer supports GBM malignancy in both murine and patient derived models. Single cell RNA sequencing along with whole cell and cell source traceable ribosome profiling reveal that transferred ribosomes are translationally active and selectively reprogram the tumor translatome, prioritizing cell-cycle genes and driving interferon-response-mediated immune evasion. Through a genome wide CRISPR screen, we identify INTS12 as a critical mediator of ribosome transfer. Genetic inactivation or AAV-mediated knockdown of INTS12 impairs ribosome uptake, curbs translation and proliferation, remodels the immunosuppressive landscape, and extends survival in orthotopic models. Our study uncovers a parasitic translation-support mechanism in GBM, establishing INTS12 as a therapeutic vulnerability to disrupt ribosome transfer.
— Source: bioRxiv Subject Collection: Cancer Biology

item.title: [2.1] Therapeutic Targeting of the TGFβ Pathway Augments CAR T cell Efficacy in Glioblastoma
item.description:
Chimeric Antigen Receptor (CAR) T therapy represents a promising approach to improve outcomes for patients with high-grade gliomas (HGG). Recently, we reported on a phase I trial assessing the local delivery of CAR T cells for HGG. Despite notable clinical benefits to CAR T treatment, clinical responses were highly variable between patients. Here we report that TGF{beta} levels in the tumor cavity fluid (TCF) decreased following CAR T treatment and that lower TGF{beta} levels positively correlated with improved patient responses to CAR T therapy. Patients were stratified based on baseline TGF{beta} levels in the TCF before CAR T therapy. Single-cell RNA sequencing of patient tumor tissues identified significant upregulation of genes associated with angiogenesis and epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition, and IL6 and SLRP pathways in TGF{beta} high patients, while IL2, chemokine signaling and NK-mediated cytotoxicity pathways were significantly upregulated in TGF{beta} low patients. Preclinically, we demonstrated that systemic treatment with a TGF{beta}R1 inhibitor markedly improved CAR T efficacy in syngeneic murine glioma models, correlating with changes in the tumor microenvironment (TME) that benefited both endogenous and CAR T cell phenotype and trafficking. Further studies demonstrated that inhibition of the TGF{beta} pathway in CAR T cells, through either TGF{beta}R1 inhibitor or CRISPR/Cas9 knockout of TGF{beta}R2 (TGF{beta}R2-KO), significantly enhanced CAR T cell expansion and antitumor activity. Collectively, our clinical and preclinical findings strongly indicate that targeting the TGF{beta} pathway could significantly enhance CAR T therapy for patients with high-grade gliomas.
— Source: bioRxiv Subject Collection: Cancer Biology

item.title: [2.5] DNA-PK enforces the S/G2 checkpoint in ATM-deficient cells to limit ATR inhibitor efficacy
item.description:
ATR inhibition has been proposed as a strategy for tumors under replication stress or those harboring ATM deficiency. However, anti-tumor activity is limited by DNA-PK and ATM compensation. Here, we have delineated distinct roles for DNA-PK and ATM during ATR inhibitor exposure. Both kinases are activated in a cell cycle-dependent manner at the S/G2 boundary following ATR inhibition. DNA-PK imposes the S/G2 checkpoint and promotes completion of DNA replication, whereas ATM detects persistent aberrant DNA replication structures with associated DNA damage in late S and G2/M to establish a G2/M checkpoint promoting DNA repair. In ATM-deficient cells and patient tumors, DNA-PK is activated following ATR inhibition and assumes greater versatility by not only enforcing the S/G2 checkpoint but also by detecting aberrant replication structures in S phase in place of ATM, allowing cells to tolerate ATR inhibition. Consequently, DNA-PK inhibition synergizes with ATR inhibition in ATM-deficient cells and enhances ATR inhibitor efficacy in ATM-deficient PDX models. These data support clinical evaluation of combined ATR and DNA-PK inhibition in ATM-deficient cancers.
— Source: bioRxiv Subject Collection: Cancer Biology

item.title: [2.6] Systematic analysis of genetic vulnerabilities caused by chromosome loss events in cancer
item.description:
Chromosome loss events are common across tumor types but rarely occur in normal tissue, raising the possibility that these alterations could be exploited as cancer-specific therapeutic vulnerabilities. Here, we integrate genome-scale CRISPR screening data with chromosome-level copy number profiles from 1,150 cancer cell lines and identify 389 dependencies that are selectively associated with individual chromosome loss events. The most significant vulnerabilities uncovered by our analysis are paralogous gene pairs, in which the loss of a paralog on an aneuploid chromosome establishes a unique dependency on its redundant paralog encoded elsewhere in the genome. We experimentally validate two paralog dependencies: loss of chromosome 8p, which encodes the phosphatase PPP2CB, creates a specific dependency on its paralog PPP2CA, while loss of the Y chromosome, which encodes the helicase DDX3Y, creates a specific dependency on its paralog DDX3X. Systematic benchmarking of CRISPR screening data indicates that the selective dependency on DDX3X in loss-of-Y cells exceeds other published aneuploidy-associated vulnerabilities and matches or exceeds most clinically-validated biomarker-target relationships. Furthermore, we found that the acute degradation of DDX3X was sufficient to trigger apoptosis in vitro and tumor regressions in mice. Collectively, these findings establish chromosome loss as a recurrent source of biomarker-defined therapeutic targets, identify paralog insufficiency as a general vulnerability in aneuploid cells, and provide in vivo proof-of-concept for targeting DDX3X in cancers with Y chromosome loss.
— Source: bioRxiv Subject Collection: Cancer Biology

item.title: [1.9] Transient Splicing-Associated Isoform Remodeling Defines Early MAPKi Resistance Adaptation in Melanoma
item.description:
A long-standing question in targeted therapy resistance is how tumor cells rapidly enter drug-tolerant states before stable resistance emerges. In BRAF-mutant melanoma, early adaptation to MAPK inhibitor (MAPKi) therapy is accompanied by profound phenotypic plasticity, yet the molecular mechanisms that enable this transition remain poorly understood. Here, we show that MAPKi adaptation is characterized by a transient transcript isoform remodeling that is largely invisible to conventional gene-expression analysis. We integrated and analyzed multiple different datasets, including bulk and single-cell RNA-seq datasets from melanoma cell lines, murine models, patient-derived xenografts and patient tumors, spanning no-treatment, on-treatment/minimal residual disease, and acquired-resistant states. We find that differential transcript usage peaks during the adaptive on-treatment phase and then is markedly attenuated when resistance was established. These dynamics were conserved across experimental systems and supported by independent exon-usage analyses. Notably, most genes undergoing differential transcript usage showed no corresponding change in total gene expression, and genes with isoform-level changes more strongly highlighted MAPKi resistance-associated pathways, including PI3K/AKT/mTOR and receptor tyrosine kinase signaling. Further, classifiers trained on cell-line transcript-usage features identified the adaptive state more accurately than gene-expression-based models in independent PDX and patient datasets. Interestingly, MAPKi-associated isoform changes recapitulated melanoblast-associated developmental splicing programs and were linked to a few key splicing regulators. Together, these findings identify an underappreciated regulatory layer connecting drug tolerance, developmental plasticity, and acquired resistance. item.title: [1.7] Optimized dosing of spatially heterogeneous radiopharmaceutical therapy reprograms poorly immunogenic tumors to enhance response to immune checkpoint blockade

item.title: [1.7] Spatially enforced engagement of PD-1⁺ T cells with AXL⁺ cells reprograms the tumor microenvironment and overcomes anti-PD-1 resistance

Background: AXL overexpression promotes tumor-cell plasticity, local immune suppression, and resistance to PD-1 blockade. Conclusion: BiTE-AXL/PD-1 promotes physical proximity between PD-1+ T cells and AXL+ cells, enhances antitumor immune responses, and remodels the immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment. item.title: [1.5] Cancer cells acquire cysteine directly from a reduced tumor microenvironment
item.description:
The metabolic environment of a tumor is shaped by the nutrients available in its interstitial fluid, yet the redox composition of that fluid is poorly defined. Measuring sulfur metabolites in the interstitial fluid of tumors, matched healthy organs, and serum across three mouse models of cancer, we find that the tumor microenvironment (TME) is a chemically reduced compartment in which free cysteine predominates over its oxidized form, cystine. This is especially pronounced in the lung TME, where cystine is nearly absent. We further show that lung cancer cells take up cysteine and cystine with comparable efficiency and proliferate on cysteine alone, and that the abundant glutathione in the TME helps keep cysteine reduced through disulfide exchange. In a medium formulated to match the sulfur composition of the lung tumor interstitial fluid, cells become independent of cystine import through xCT. Cells cultured in this medium were resistant to glutaminase inhibitors, oxidants and ferroptosis inducers, and better maintained NADPH levels under oxidative challenge. These findings suggest that standard culture conditions overestimate the dependence of cancer cells on cystine uptake and their vulnerability to oxidative stress-targeting therapies.

item.title: [2.0] Targeting alpha-ketoglutarate starvation within the tumor-immune microenvironment rescues T cell effector function in cancer immunotherapy
item.description:
Given its status as the leading cause of global cancer mortality, there is a critical need to enhance immunotherapy strategies for lung cancer to overcome widespread resistance to current treatments. Immunotherapy recruits the patient's immune system to attack and destroy cancer cells. While highly effective in a subset of patients, chronic exposure of immune cells to cancer cells leads to a progressive loss of effector T cell function and progression of T cell exhaustion; now considered two well-established hallmarks of immunotherapy resistance. The tumor-immune microenvironment (TIME)-driven differentiation into the exhausted T cell phenotype is marked by a loss of metabolic plasticity and epigenome-wide changes in distribution of repressive histone marks such as histone H3 subunit methylation at lysine 27 (H3K27me3). Here, we studied how these processes are connected to metabolite availability within the TIME. In vitro, chronic antigen stimulation and hypoxia led to rapid loss of effector function, associated with a suppression of alpha-ketoglutarate (aKG) intracellular concentrations in T cells. Supplementation of cell-permeable aKG led to a rescue of effector cytokine production and to improved cytotoxic capacity despite chronic antigen stimulation and hypoxia. Increased intracellular aKG levels restored the activity of H3K27 demethylases UTX and JMJD3, consistent with epigenome-wide decreased H3K27me3. In vivo, dietary supplementation with commercially available calcium-aKG (Ca-aKG) supplements led to an elevation of serum and intratumoral aKG levels associated with a significant increase of immunotherapy effectiveness in mouse models of NSCLC. Clinical samples from patients with NSCLC contained significantly decreased serum aKG levels in older NSCLC patients (>65 years of age). Analysis identified a novel association between serum aKG levels and poor immunotherapy response. Thus, our work demonstrates that intratumoral metabolite starvation can be therapeutically exploited to improve immunotherapy outcomes in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC).

item.title: [2.1] Molecular glue degraders of CK1α remodel lysosomes and limit ferroptosis in glioblastoma stem-like cells

Glioblastoma stem-like cells (GSCs) are highly plastic tumor cells that drive initiation, progression and therapeutic resistance. Although lysosomal homeostasis has emerged as a critical determinant of GSC fitness, the molecular mechanisms regulating this compartment remain incompletely understood. item.title: [1.6] Aquaporin-4 Regulates Edema, Sustains Astrocyte Differentiation, and Constrains Immunosuppressive Remodeling in Glioblastoma
item.description:
Vasogenic cerebral edema is a severe complication that affects most patients with glioblastoma (GBM). It leads to an increase in intracranial pressure, neurological deficits, and increased mortality rates. While there is considerable research on edema formation, the molecular and cellular mechanisms of edema resolution in GBM, particularly in response to dexamethasone or other anti-edema therapies, remain largely undefined. Our findings demonstrate that the water channel aquaporin-4 (AQP4), a key regulator of brain water homeostasis, is upregulated in human GBM compared to the normal brain. AQP4 expression correlates with peritumoral edema in GBM patients, with the classical (CL) GBM subtype exhibiting the highest AQP4 levels but the lowest edema content relative to the proneural (PN) and mesenchymal (MES) subtypes. Using the RCAS/tv-a system, we generated de novo GBM with defined driver mutations in Aqp4-proficient and -deficient mice. Loss of Aqp4 shortened survival and exacerbated edema, accompanied by reduced astrocytic coverage within the tumor core, but not at the tumor margin. Single-cell RNA-sequencing and spatial transcriptomics revealed that Aqp4 loss reprograms astrocytes toward an immature, progenitor-like state and alters their crosstalk with other cell types in the GBM microenvironment. Additionally, loss of Aqp4 skewed myeloid populations toward immunosuppressive phenotypes while reducing lymphoid infiltration. Treatment with anti-VEGFA antibody, an established anti-edema therapy, increased expression of Aqp4 and reduced vessel leakage, underscoring the role of AQP4 in the therapeutic modulation of brain water balance. Overall, this study highlights the important role of AQP4 in resolving edema and its critical function in maintaining astrocyte identity and shaping the immune landscape of GBM.

item.title: [2.0] Targeting IGF2BP1 Creates a Mitotic Vulnerability in Colorectal Carcinoma
item.description:
Background Mitotic dysregulation is a common feature of colorectal cancer (CRC), yet the contribution of post-transcriptional mechanisms remain incompletely understood. We investigated how the oncofetal RNA-binding protein IGF2BP1 supports mitotic integrity and exposes therapeutic vulnerabilities in CRC. Methods We integrated patient cohort analyses with genetic and pharmacological perturbation of IGF2BP1, transcriptomics, proteomics, RNA-binding assays and functional studies. Xenografts assessed tumor formation, while BTYNB-paclitaxel responses were examined in CRC cell lines and patient-derived organoids. Results IGF2BP1 expression was elevated in CRC, increased with tumor stage, and associated with poor survival and proliferative gene signatures. Genetic depletion or pharmacological inhibition of IGF2BP1 impaired cell viability, induced mitotic abnormalities, and promoted apoptosis, whereas its re-expression enhanced tumor formation in vivo. Integrated molecular analyses identified the chromosomal passenger complex (CPC) as a previously unrecognized downstream target of IGF2BP1. IGF2BP1 bound transcripts encoding CPC components and its depletion consistently reduced their expression across multiple cancer cell models. BTYNB disrupted IGF2BP1 association with INCENP, CDCA8, and BIRC5 transcripts and accelerated INCENP mRNA decay. Functionally, INCENP depletion recapitulated the mitotic defects and impaired viability observed upon IGF2BP1 inhibition. Exploiting this mitotic vulnerability, BTYNB synergized with paclitaxel in CRC cell lines and across four independent IGF2BP1-positive patient-derived organoid models. Conclusions Our findings uncover an IGF2BP1-dependent post-transcriptional regulatory mechanism sustaining CPC expression and mitotic integrity in CRC. Targeting this mechanism exposes a therapeutically exploitable mitotic vulnerability and provides a rationale for combining IGF2BP1 inhibition with microtubule-targeting agents.

To address this challenge, we used structure-guided directed evolution and yeast surface display to affinity-mature the anti-MUC1-Tn antibody 5E5, generating variants with high-affinity dual recognition of MUC1-Tn and MUC1-STn. Co-crystal structures revealed that heavy-chain CDR loops cooperatively engage the GalNAc moiety primarily through hydrogen-bonding networks, in which HCDR3 residue 98 fine-tunes glycoform preference: Tyr98 favors MUC1-Tn recognition, whereas His98 enhances MUC1-STn engagement, while both support high-affinity recognition of both glycoforms. Together, these findings establish functional glycoform coverage as a design principle for antibody engineering, whereby a single paratope is optimized to recognize a defined spectrum of tumor-associated glycoforms while preserving antigen specificity, providing a strategy to overcome glycan heterogeneity in solid tumor immunotherapy.

item.title: [1.7] Expanding Therapeutic Target Space from Genes to Disease-Relevant Molecular Forms with Agent3Diso
item.description:
Therapeutic targets are commonly defined at the gene or canonical protein level, yet therapeutic effects are ultimately exerted through specific molecular states operating in specific biological contexts. Alternative splicing generates diverse RNA and translated protein forms whose functional consequences, disease relevance, and therapeutic vulnerabilities can differ substantially within the same gene. Resolving these disease-relevant molecular forms creates opportunities for selective intervention across complementary RNA- and protein-directed modalities, but requires reasoning across tightly coupled molecular layers, heterogeneous evidence, explicit biological constraints, and modality-specific therapeutic requirements. Here, we present Agent3Diso, a hybrid deterministic--agent multimodal framework for molecular-form-resolved therapeutic discovery. Agent3Diso establishes cross-layer molecular coherence from transcript identity and translation to structure, function, and disease context; enforces explicit molecular and therapeutic constraints through deterministic computation; and applies specialized agentic reasoning to evidence synthesis, mechanistic interpretation, conflict resolution, hypothesis critique, and experimental design. The framework evaluates therapeutic opportunities across multiple intervention modalities and translates prioritized disease-relevant molecular states into traceable hypotheses linking molecular identity, therapeutic rationale, modality, concrete intervention, uncertainty, and experimental validation. By integrating molecular resolution with constraint-aware and modality-conditioned agentic reasoning, Agent3Diso provides a framework for extending therapeutic discovery beyond gene-level targets toward disease-relevant molecular forms.

item.title: [2.7] DIRAS3 broadly suppresses signaling from diverse oncogenic KRAS hotspot variants through an inhibitory interface
item.description:
Despite major advances in KRAS-directed therapies, broadly suppressing oncogenic KRAS signaling across diverse hotspot variants remains an unmet challenge. Here, we identify an endogenous inhibitory mechanism that suppresses signaling across the major oncogenic KRAS hotspot classes while largely sparing basal wild-type KRAS, revealing activation-state-selective inhibition. Using genetically controlled RASless reconstitution models, complementary cancer cell validation, structure-function analyses, molecular dynamics-based membrane topology modeling, and ultrastructural imaging, we show that dual lipid modification constrains DIRAS3 membrane topology, enabling an 5-encoded inhibitory interface to engage activated KRAS, disrupt signaling-competent membrane assemblies, and suppress downstream signaling. Structure-function analyses establish this interface as a critical determinant of DIRAS3-mediated KRAS inhibition. A conformationally constrained 5 mimetic recapitulates full-length DIRAS3 activity, broadly suppressing MAPK and PI3K signaling across multiple oncogenic KRAS variants, including Q61 mutants with reduced sensitivity to current tri-complex RAS(ON) inhibitors. Mechanistically, immunoprecipitation shows that the 5 mimetic reduces KRAS association with both RAF1 and p110 similarly across G12 and Q61 mutants, whereas RMC-7977 reduces inhibition of p110 association with Q61 KRAS. The 5 mimetic also disrupts KRAS nanocluster organization and inhibits tumor growth in vivo. These findings identify a targetable inhibitory interface within DIRAS3 and establish mimicry of an endogenous KRAS suppressor as a mechanistically distinct strategy for broad KRAS inhibition.

item.title: [1.9] Testis-Specific MAGEA3/6 Regulate Glycolysis to Promote Metabolic Flexibility and Reveal Therapeutic Vulnerabilities in Pancreatic Cancer Cells
item.description:
Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) is an aggressive tumor characterized by metabolic plasticity that enables cancer cells to survive nutrient deprivation and therapeutic stress. Melanoma-associated antigens A3 and A6 (MAGEA3/6), members of the cancer-testis antigen family with a previously identified protective role in spermatogenesis during nutritional stress, have been implicated in cancer progression and metabolic regulation. However, their contribution to metabolic adaptation in pancreatic cancer remains poorly understood. Here, we investigated the molecular mechanisms underlying MAGEA3/6-mediated resistance to glycolytic inhibition using complementary gain- and loss-of-function models, pharmacological inhibition of metabolic pathways, cellular metabolic assays, and integrated transcriptomic, proteomic, metabolomic, and lipidomic analyses. MAGEA3/6 expression enhanced resistance to 2-deoxy-D-glucose (2-DG), with MAGEA6-expressing MIA PaCa-2 cells exhibiting a greater than 2.5-fold increase in the half-maximal inhibitory concentration (IC50). Conversely, MAGEA3/6 depletion reduced clonogenic growth and migration and increased sensitivity to 2-DG. Resistance persisted despite pharmacological inhibition of mTORC1, the pentose phosphate pathway, or glutaminase, suggesting metabolic adaptations beyond these pathways. Unexpectedly, MAGEA6 expression was associated with increased rather than decreased AMPK1 protein abundance, contrasting with previously reported MAGEA3/6-mediated AMPK degradation and suggesting context-dependent regulation of this master regulator of cellular metabolism. MAGEA6 also reduced hexokinase HK1 and HK2 abundance while increasing several downstream glycolytic enzymes, revealing discordant regulation of glycolysis. Seahorse analyses and integrated multi-omics profiling identified extensive remodeling of mitochondrial metabolism, glutamine-aspartate metabolism, phospholipid composition, lipid storage, and redox homeostasis. item.title: [2.6] Oncogenic KRAS-MAPK signaling sustains a CD73 dependent therapeutic vulnerability in pancreatic cancer
item.description:
Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) is predominantly driven by oncogenic KRAS signaling and sustained by a desmoplastic, immunosuppressive microenvironment limiting therapeutic response. item.title: [2.2] GLP1R agonists and vorasidenib converge on peroxynitrite-mediated cytotoxicity in mutant IDH glioma
item.description:
Mutations in isocitrate dehydrogenase 1 or 2 (mIDH) generate the oncometabolite D-2-hydroxyglutarate that drives tumorigenesis in a distinct molecular class of gliomas. The mIDH inhibitor vorasidenib slows tumor growth, but disease progression remains a challenge, identifying a need for strategies that deepen and prolong therapeutic response. Here, we show that glucagon-like peptide-1R (GLP1R) agonists synergize with vorasidenib in patient-derived and murine models of mIDH glioma. Mechanistically, GLP1R agonists activate cAMP-protein kinase A signaling and induce nitric oxide synthase 1-dependent nitric oxide production in mIDH glioma cells. Nitric oxide inhibits aconitase and ribonucleotide reductase via S-nitrosylation, thereby disrupting the tricarboxylic acid cycle, depleting deoxyribonucleotides, blocking DNA synthesis, and exerting a cytostatic inhibition of tumor cell proliferation. Concomitantly, vorasidenib relieves D-2HG-driven suppression of pyruvate dehydrogenase, thereby increasing mitochondrial superoxide production and suppressing proliferation without cytotoxicity. When combined, GLP1R agonist-induced nitric oxide and vorasidenib-induced superoxide converge to generate peroxynitrite, which damages lipids and DNA, and triggers apoptosis in mIDH glioma cells. Combining a GLP1R agonist with vorasidenib recapitulates these metabolic and pharmacodynamic effects in mice bearing intracranial mIDH tumors, induces tumor regression, and significantly prolongs survival relative to each monotherapy in vivo. Collectively, our studies demonstrate that GLP1R agonism and mIDH inhibition induce distinct alterations in mitochondrial redox metabolism that converge to produce synergistic cytotoxicity and provide a mechanistic basis for clinical evaluation of this therapeutic strategy in patients with mIDH glioma.

item.title: [1.8] Dissecting KEAP1-NRF2 interactions: Structural and functional impact of cancer-associated KEAP1 mutants
item.description:
Kelch-like ECH-associated protein 1 (KEAP1) is a cysteine-rich substrate adaptor for the CUL3-RBX1 E3 ubiquitin ligase complex, primarily regulating the transcription factor NRF2. By promoting NRF2 degradation under basal conditions, KEAP1 maintains redox homeostasis, while oxidative or electrophilic stress disrupts this regulation, enabling NRF2 activation of cytoprotective genes. Dysregulation of the KEAP1-NRF2 pathway, often through KEAP1 mutations, is implicated in cancer, where constitutive NRF2 activation promotes tumour growth, chemoresistance, and metabolic reprogramming. In this study, we investigated structural and functional consequences of three representative KEAP1 mutants R470C (superbinder), G480W (hypomorphic), and R554Q (null allele) using thermal shift assays (TSA), microscale thermophoresis (MST), isothermal calorimetry (ITC), and X-ray crystallography, complemented by AlphaFold3 modelling. TSA revealed that while inhibitor-induced thermal stability shifts followed similar pattern across mutants, baseline stability varied significantly, with R554Q showing the largest destabilisation. MST and ITC confirmed mutant-specific alterations in NRF2 ETGE peptide binding affinity, consistent with their known functional classifications. Structures of mutant-inhibitor and mutant-peptide complexes showed remarkable structural similarity to native KEAP1, with preserved inhibitor and peptide binding orientations despite residue substitutions. Spatial mapping of reported KEAP1 mutations revealed clustering of superbinder mutations near the IVR interface, while most loss-of-function variants localised within the KELCH domain. Our findings provide a detailed structural and biophysical characterization of clinically relevant KEAP1 mutations, offering mechanistic insights into their functional diversity. This work advances the understanding of KEAP1 mutation effects, with implications for therapeutic targeting of the KEAP1-NRF2 pathway in cancer.

item.title: [1.9] A comprehensive temporal proteome and phosphoproteome dataset of Y1 adrenocortical cells under FGF2 stimulation and SOS inhibition
item.description:
The Y1 mouse adrenocortical tumor cell line is a classic model for cancer studies and ACTH mediated steroidogenesis. The KRAS gene amplification and SOS mediated activation sustain elevated ERK levels, which drive the tumor phenotype of this cell line. In addition, the mitogen FGF2 induces atypical cytotoxic stress and consequent cell death rather than proliferation in this system, imposing a strong perturbation on KRAS ERK signaling dynamics. Recent research from our group revealed that SOS is not solely responsible for KRAS activation in the Y1 cells, indicating a more complex regulatory landscape of GEFs and GAPs. This motivated the generation of a comprehensive time resolved proteome (DIA) and TMT phosphoproteome (DDA) in a 0 to 30 minute time course under FGF2 stimulation or combined with SOS inhibitor, with the presence or absence of FBS stimulation, in technical triplicate using Q Exactive and Thermo Lumos mass spectrometers, respectively. This dataset can enable latent mechanisms between the life and death switch caused by FGF2 signaling and the alternate stress response caused by impaired SOS dependent activation. This analysis yielded 14,512 phosphosites and 8,919 protein groups, where 10,471 phosphosites and 111 protein groups showed differential abundance with statistical significance (limma, FDR < 0.05%). This dataset provides a versatile resource for downstream applications, which includes dynamic modeling such as ordinary differential equation based frameworks, for which temporal datasets remain scarce. The data contained in this preprint will be available on JPOST Repo after the publication.

item.title: [2.7] ESCRT-dependent YAP degradation by AKT blockade overcomes adaptive resistance to RAS(ON) inhibition in pancreatobiliary cancer
item.description:

item.title: [2.3] A First-in-Class LZK Inhibitor Suppresses Tumor Growth and Potentiates EGFR and PI3K Pathway Blockade in Head and Neck and Esophageal Cancers
item.description:
Amplification of MAP3K13, which encodes leucine zipper-bearing kinase (LZK), occurs in a substantial proportion of head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC) and esophageal squamous cell carcinoma (ESCC), highlighting LZK as an attractive therapeutic target[1,2]. Here, we describe the design and optimization of a novel series of LZK inhibitors through systematic modification of the dual leucine zipper kinase (DLK) inhibitor GNE-3511[3]. Pharmacologic inhibition of LZK by compound #63 effectively suppressed kinase activity, reduced expression of the oncogenic effector c-MYC, and inhibited the viability of HNSCC and ESCC cells at low concentrations. The combination significantly enhanced antitumor activity relative to compound #63 alone and improved the efficacy of PAC-XL. item.title: [2.2] Radiation-Induced Collagen I&III Accumulation Drives Immunosuppressive Evolution in Recurrent Glioblastoma
item.description:

Combining buparlisib with PD-1 blockade further prolonged survival, whereas PD-1 blockade alone was ineffective. These findings establish a mechanistic connection between recurrence-associated matrix remodeling and immune suppression, and identify COL I&III-driven signaling as a therapeutic vulnerability for improving immunotherapy in recurrent GBM.

item.title: [2.7] Pharmacologic inhibition of OLIG2 by CT-179 disrupts mitotic progression and enhances standard-of-care chemoradiotherapy in glioblastoma
item.description:
Background: Glioblastoma (GBM) remains uniformly fatal. The basic helix-loop-helix transcription factor OLIG2 is universally expressed in diffuse glioma, sustains the tumor-propagating stem-like fraction, and opposes p53-mediated genotoxic responses, but has historically been considered undruggable. We characterized CT-179, a brain-penetrant small-molecule OLIG2 inhibitor, as a candidate therapeutic for GBM. Methods: Target engagement was assessed by cellular thermal shift assay, differential scanning fluorimetry, crosslinking, and electrophoretic mobility shift assay. Anti-tumor activity was evaluated across eleven patient-derived GBM cell lines, in zebrafish oligodendrocyte precursor cell (OPC)-derived tumors, and orthotopic and subcutaneous GBM models, including combinations with radiotherapy plus temozolomide and with selective Bcl-2 family inhibitors. Results: CT-179 engaged OLIG2 and altered the conformation of dimerized OLIG2 on chromatin without preventing dimerization or fully displacing OLIG2 from DNA. CT-179 reduced OLIG2-positive OPCs and OPC-derived tumors in zebrafish and inhibited proliferation across all eleven GBM lines (IC50 < 360 nM), depleting the stem-like fraction and inducing apoptosis through mitotic catastrophe, mitotic slippage, or a hybrid response. RNA-seq across three patient-derived glioma stem cell lines identified {beta}-tubulin gene isoforms as the most strongly CT-179-down-regulated transcripts at the early time point and showed correlated {beta}-tubulin and OLIG2 expression in TCGA glioblastoma specimens. Combination with the Mcl-1 inhibitor S63845 or the Bcl-2/Bcl-xL/Bcl-w inhibitor ABT-737 produced greater-than-additive cytotoxicity. Conclusions: CT-179 is a brain-penetrant inhibitor of an established GBM driver with single-agent and combination activity across several orthotopic models, supporting clinical development for GBM and translational evaluation in other OLIG2-dependent CNS malignancies.

However, quantitative PET assessment of PARP1 in infiltrative tumors with a preserved blood-brain barrier remains an unmet need. Standardized uptake value ratios (SUVRs) for tumors were calculated using the contralateral region as reference and compared with distribution volume ratios (DVRs) calculated using kinetic modeling. Conclusion: [18F]Itareparib showed brain penetration, high in vivo metabolic stability, reversible binding kinetics, and PARP1-specific tumor uptake. item.title: [1.8] Droplet-based organoid screens enable high-throughput identification of cancer vulnerabilities
item.description:

item.title: [1.8] Targeting proteasome composition reprograms tumor-intrinsic inflammation through selective degradation of STAT1

Proteasome regulatory particles determine cellular protein degradation capacities. item.title: [1.9] Rapid Micronucleus-Sequencing (RaMN-Seq) Reveals Patterns of Bias in Induced and Spontaneous Chromosomal Instability
item.description:
Micronuclei are extra-nuclear structures formed following aberrant chromosome mis-segregation. Due to abnormal membrane features, micronuclei are liable to membrane rupture and are proposed as an important intermediate of extreme genome evolution events in cancer such as chromothripsis. Studying the features and contents of micronuclei can be informative about the underlying defective genomic instability process, but current purification strategies are time-consuming and require specialised methods. We developed Rapid MicroNucleus sequencing (RaMN-seq), a rapid (~2 hour), kit-style micronucleus purification strategy coupled to single micronucleus low-pass DNA sequencing to explore the genomic contents of micronuclei. Using RaMN-Seq we recapitulate the known chromosome bias of nocodazole washout-induced chromosome mis-segregation in diploid cells. We explore the features of ruptured (cGAS-positive) and intact micronuclei, finding no substantial differences in chromosomal contents or sizes between rupture states. Finally, we extend RaMN-Seq to cancer models, demonstrating the ability to rapidly explore features of chromosomal instability in cancer cell lines and fresh-frozen tumour samples. Overall, RaMN-Seq allows simple, rapid purification of micronuclei from a range of sources, and offers an inexpensive alternative to single cell genome sequencing to examine properties and chromosomal identities of genetic material affected by chromosomal instability.

item.title: [1.8] Tobacco Carcinogen Induces Persistent DNA Damage and Homologous Recombination Dysregulation in Pancreatic Ductal Carcinogenesis
item.description:
Cigarette smoking is a well-established risk factor for the development of pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC), yet the mechanisms by which tobacco carcinogens, such as Nicotine-Derived Nitrosamine Ketone (NNK), drive pancreatic carcinogenesis remain incompletely understood. We investigated the impact of NNK on pancreatic epithelium by treating human pancreatic ductal epithelial cells (HPDE6-E6E7; H6c7) with NNK for 5 or 50 days followed by genome-wide RNA sequencing, qRT-PCR, immunofluorescence, comet assay, and {gamma}H2AX ELISA. We assessed {gamma}H2AX by immunohistochemistry in human PDAC tissue microarrays and in TCGA-PAAD datasets to identify clinical correlates. Acute NNK exposure (5 days) induced DNA double-strand breaks and activated ATM-{gamma}H2AX signaling, accompanied by increased RAD51 and BRCA2 recruitment, consistent with activation of homologous recombination (HR)-mediated DNA repair. In contrast, chronic NNK exposure (50 days) resulted in persistent DNA damage signaling and transcriptional upregulation of HR-associated genes, including RAD51, BRCA1, BRCA2, FANCD2, and PLK1. Despite sustained accumulation of RAD51- and BRCA2-positive repair foci, chronic NNK exposure was associated with altered RAD51 localization, persistent DNA damage, and chromosomal instability, suggesting dysregulation of HR repair fidelity during prolonged genotoxic stress. {gamma}H2AX expression was significantly elevated in NNK-treated cells, KRAS-driven premalignant pancreatic lesions, and pancreatic tissues from smokers. Increased {gamma}H2AX expression correlated with tumor progression and poor overall survival, while elevated RAD51 expression was associated with adverse outcomes in patients with PDAC. Collectively, these findings reveal a biphasic DNA damage response to NNK characterized by early activation of ATM-{gamma}H2AX-dependent DNA repair followed by persistent DNA damage signaling, dysregulated HR repair, and genomic instability during chronic exposure. Tobacco-induced disruption of DNA repair homeostasis may represent a key mechanism driving pancreatic carcinogenesis and supports {gamma}H2AX as a clinically relevant prognostic biomarker in tobacco-associated PDAC.

In contrast, trophectoderm-associated programs expressed by tumour cells were coupled with worse overall survival in breast cancer and melanoma. These trophectoderm-associated programs were associated with MYBL2-driven cell cycle progression, oxidative phosphorylation and biosynthetic pathways. Integration with cancer cell line dependency data uncovered MYBL2 and FOXM1 as therapeutic vulnerabilities specifically in trophectoderm-high cancers. These findings reveal that the stage of embryonic development a tumour resembles has profound and opposing prognostic consequences and uncover actionable gene dependencies that could be exploited therapeutically.

item.title: [1.6] Mechanosensors Collaborate to Regulate DNA Damage Repair in Hepatocellular Carcinoma
item.description:
Abstract Increased matrix stiffness is a biomechanical feature of hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) that functions as an important promoting factor driving tumor progression. Specifically, SDC4 and PKD2 modulated matrix stiffness–increased BANF1 nuclear translocation by increasing protein phosphatase 2A assembly and activity. These findings not only expand the theoretical understanding of matrix stiffness–regulated DDR but also offer a screening/identification approach for mechanosensors in cancer. Significance: Matrix stiffness enhances DNA repair via dual pathways in hepatocellular carcinoma, suggesting that targeting mechanosensory cross-talk could be a potential strategy to overcome cytotoxic drug resistance.

item.title: [1.7] ARID1A Stimulates Notch-TLL1 Signaling to Induce Cancer-Associated Fibroblast Activation and Intrahepatic Cholangiocarcinoma Development
item.description:
Abstract Intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma (ICC) is a lethal hepatic malignancy characterized by a prominent desmoplastic stroma. In this study, we demonstrated that AT-rich interactive domain-containing protein 1A (ARID1A), a core component of the Switch/Sucrose (SWI/SNF) protein complex, is upregulated in ICC and plays an oncogenic role. Mechanistically, ARID1A stabilized NICD1 protein by inhibiting AMPK-dependent autophagy and lysosomal degradation, thereby sustaining Notch signaling. Tolloid-like 1 (TLL1), a metalloproteinase that promotes collagen maturation, was found to be a downstream effector of ARID1A/Notch signaling. Specifically, TLL1 derived from ICC cells activated hepatic stellate cells (HSC) and thus promoted tumor progression. Accordingly, ablation of TLL1 attenuated cancer-associated fibroblast infiltration, collagen accumulation, and tumor progression. Moreover, virtual screening of a bioactive compound library identified acarbose, an effective medicine for glycemic control, as a potent inhibitor of TLL1. Pharmacologic inhibition of TLL1 with acarbose suppressed HSC activation, collagen deposition, and tumor development. Collectively, these results establish a tumor-promoting ARID1A–Notch–TLL1 axis in ICC and reveal acarbose as a potential precision therapy for patients with ARID1A-high ICC. Significance: The ARID1A-Notch-TLL1 axis promotes hepatic stellate cell activation and intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma development, which can be targeted with acarbose as a TLL1 inhibitor to suppress tumor progression.

item.title: [1.9] Single-Cell Analysis of Residual Esophageal Squamous Cell Carcinoma after Neoadjuvant Immunochemotherapy Reveals TFAM-Mediated Immunoregulation in Dendritic Cells
item.description:
Abstract Neoadjuvant immunochemotherapy (nICT) has emerged as a promising neoadjuvant strategy for esophageal squamous cell carcinoma (ESCC). Identification of the factors affecting responsiveness to nICT could help further improve treatment efficacy. In this study, we performed single-cell analysis on 14 patients with ESCC undergoing nICT and revealed tumor microenvironment (TME) features associated with differential treatment responses. Nonnegative matrix factorization (NMF) identified five coordinated cellular programs with distinct response associations. Specifically, the NMF3 program, mainly comprising immunosuppressive cell subsets, was enriched in the minimal or no pathologic tumor regression [tumor regression staging 3 (TRS3)] group, in which regulatory T cells (Treg) and dendritic cells (DC) exhibited a close correlation. In addition, elevated expression of mitochondrial transcription factor A (TFAM) in DCs was associated with increased Treg infiltration in the TRS3 group. A myeloid-specific Tfam knockout mouse model showed that TFAM deficiency reversed the immunosuppressive TME, inhibited tumor growth, and enhanced the response to anti–programmed cell death protein 1 therapy in ESCC. Mechanistically, TFAM deficiency in DCs activated the stimulator of IFN genes (STING)–TBK1–IRF3 pathway, thereby promoting DC maturation to enhance antitumor immunity. Overall, this study characterized the TME in residual ESCC after nICT and revealed an association between elevated TFAM expression in DCs and poor responsiveness to nICT. These findings indicate the critical role of TFAM deficiency in DCs in activating antitumor immunity, highlighting the potential of targeting TFAM to improve the efficacy of immunotherapy and optimize therapeutic strategies. Significance: TFAM mediates dendritic cell activation through the STING-TBK1-IRF3 pathway and is associated with responsiveness to neoadjuvant immunochemotherapy in esophageal squamous cell carcinoma, identifying TFAM as a putative immunotherapeutic target and biomarker.
— Source: Cancer Research Current Issue

item.title: [2.5] MEKing Room: On the Quest for New Sources of Therapeutic Index in RAS/MAPK-Driven Cancers
item.description:
The RAS/MAPK pathway is among the most frequently dysregulated in human cancer, predominantly driven by activating mutations across RAS and BRAF in a broad spectrum of tumor types. The recent clinical validation of direct inhibitors of RAS, long considered undruggable, has reenergized the field and renewed focus on targeting the full RAS/MAPK axis. MEK, a central node in MAPK signaling, remains an attractive mutation-agnostic target, yet the efficacy of first-generation MEK inhibitors has been limited by pathway reactivation in tumors and by on-target, off-tissue toxicity. In this issue of Cancer Research , Kolitz and colleagues describe atebimetinib, a novel MEK inhibitor that also prevents feedback-induced MEK phosphorylation by RAF. The uniquely short plasma half-life of atebimetinib enables deep cyclic inhibition (DCI): transient but profound MEK/ERK output suppression with full recovery between doses. At each drug’s tolerability limit, atebimetinib outperformed the MEK inhibitor binimetinib across multiple RAS - and BRAF -mutant tumor models. Whether DCI or suppression of MEK phosphorylation is the primary driver of the improved therapeutic window and how atebimetinib compares with the clinical standard and other MEK-targeting agents remain important open questions, but the work makes a compelling case that novel pharmacology can unlock therapeutic spaces at targets long considered exhausted. See related article by Kolitz et al., p. 5223

item.title: [2.3] CRISPR Screening Identifies SMARCAL1 and MRN as Modulators of WRN Dependency in MSI-H Colorectal Cancer
item.description:
Abstract Microsatellite instability–high (MSI-H) colorectal cancer cells depend on the Werner syndrome helicase (WRN) to resolve cruciform DNA structures that arise from expanded TA-dinucleotide repeats. Loss of WRN induces replication stress and double-strand breaks, a vulnerability that can be recapitulated with the selective WRN inhibitor (WRNi) HRO761 in MSI-H cancer cells. To uncover the mechanisms governing sensitivity to WRN inhibition, we conducted genome-wide CRISPR/Cas9 screens in colorectal cancer cell lines treated with or without HRO761. These screens identified SMARCAL1 as a key modulator of WRN dependency. Depletion of SMARCAL1 rendered cells resistant to WRN inhibition, and rescue of this effect required the ATPase/translocase activity of SMARCAL1. Mechanistically, SMARCAL1 antagonized WRN and supported cruciform DNA structures, thereby enhancing cellular reliance on WRN. In addition, the MRE11–RAD50–NBS1 (MRN) complex, rather than MUS81 or ERCC1/XPF, was the principal mediator of cruciform DNA processing following WRN inhibition. Acute disruption of the MRN complex conferred profound resistance to WRN inhibition, whereas ataxia-telangiectasia mutated (ATM) deficiency produced a more modest resistant phenotype. Further genetic and pharmacologic epistasis analyses demonstrated that the MRN complex regulates WRNi sensitivity through both ATM-dependent signaling and MRE11 nuclease–dependent functions. Importantly, the key resistance mechanisms identified in this study were independently validated using a structurally distinct clinical-stage WRNi, VVD-214. Collectively, these findings identify the SMARCAL1–MRN–ATM axis as a critical regulator of WRN dependency and provide mechanistic insights into resistance to WRN-targeted therapy. Significance: SMARCAL1 and the MRN-ATM pathway determine sensitivity to WRN inhibition in microsatellite instability–high colorectal cancer, revealing key mechanisms of WRN dependency and potential drivers of resistance to WRN inhibitors.
— Source: Cancer Research Current Issue

item.title: [1.9] Serine Starvation Modulates mRNA Splicing through Translational Inhibition of SRSF Proteins
item.description:
Abstract Serine is a critical nutrient for cancer cell proliferation due to its numerous downstream biosynthetic functions. Given the ongoing clinical efforts to utilize dietary serine starvation as a potential therapy for serine auxotrophic tumors, it is important to understand how cancer cells respond to serine starvation. In this study, we demonstrated that serine starvation induces dramatic changes in mRNA splicing. These effects are due, in part, to reduced translation of serine-rich proteins, including the serine/arginine-rich splicing factor (SRSF) proteins that are known regulators of mRNA splicing. Indeed, translation of SRSF6 was reduced upon serine starvation in serine auxotrophic cancer cells and contributes to the RNA splicing changes seen upon serine deprivation. Furthermore, reduced SRSF6 affected DNA damage response and cell survival in the absence of exogenous serine, and modulators of RNA splicing combined with dietary serine starvation to inhibit tumor growth. Collectively, this work describes a fundamental role for serine in supporting mRNA splicing, which may have implications in the clinical efforts to bring dietary serine starvation to the clinic. Significance: Serine starvation induces changes in mRNA splicing by inhibiting translation of serine-rich proteins like SRSF6, which impacts the DNA damage response and could affect how cancer cells respond to chemotherapy.
— Source: Cancer Research Current Issue

item.title: [1.9] KRAS Mutations Reprogram RNA m 6 A Modifications to Drive CD73-Dependent Immune Evasion in Colorectal Cancer
item.description:
Abstract KRAS mutations, present in about 40% of colorectal cancers, are strongly associated with an immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment characterized by restricted immune infiltration and poor responses to immunotherapy. In this study, we found that KRAS mutations remodel the N 6 -methyladenosine (m 6 A) epitranscriptome to promote immune evasion. Methylated RNA immunoprecipitation sequencing revealed that KRAS -mutant cells exhibit increased m 6 A deposition on CD73 mRNA, enhancing its stability through IGF2BP3. TEAD4-dependent recruitment of the METTL3 methyltransferase complex induced the m 6 A modification, identifying TEAD4 as a spatial regulator of m 6 A deposition. Functionally, METTL3 knockdown in KRAS -mutant syngeneic tumors suppressed tumor growth and restored antitumor immunity by increasing CD8 + T-cell and NK cell infiltration in a CD73-dependent manner. Moreover, METTL3 inhibition synergized with anti–PD-1 therapy and a CD73 inhibitor to reduce tumor burden. Together, these findings demonstrate that KRAS-driven m 6 A remodeling is a key mechanism of immune suppression in colorectal cancer and highlight METTL3 as a promising therapeutic target. Significance: KRAS mutations suppress immune cell infiltration by increasing CD73 expression through m 6 A reprogramming driven by TEAD4-mediated relocalization of METTL3, providing a targetable axis to promote antitumor immunity.
— Source: Cancer Research Current Issue

item.title: [1.9] Regression-Associated Macrophages Recruit Natural Killer Cells That Constrain Targeted Therapy Resistance
item.description:
Abstract Targeted kinase inhibitors induce marked tumor regressions but are limited by the emergence of drug-tolerant residual disease and resistance. Although tumor-intrinsic and adaptive immune mechanisms have been extensively studied, a better understanding of the contribution of innate immunity to targeted therapy durability is needed to devise optimal treatment strategies. In this study, we showed that natural killer (NK) cells constrain targeted therapy resistance and identified a regression-associated macrophage program that promotes NK cell recruitment. In immunocompetent melanoma models that recapitulate patient treatment trajectories, tumor regression was characterized by robust NK infiltration, which transitioned to an NK-excluded residual state preceding resistance. A regression-associated macrophage subset (F4/80 high CCL5 + MHC class II + CD63 + ) contributed to NK cell recruitment via CCR2/5 signaling. Genetic depletion of macrophages using LysM-cre;iDTR mice impaired NK cell infiltration. Pharmacologic inhibition of protein tyrosine phosphatase nonreceptor type 22 (Ptpn22), a negative regulator of immune activation, reprogrammed the residual tumor microenvironment, restored NK cell recruitment, and delayed resistance onset. An analysis of data from patients with melanoma and lung cancer revealed concordant NK dynamics during therapy, linking this innate immune program to clinical outcomes. These findings identify innate immune remodeling as a key contributor to targeted therapy durability and identify NK cell recruitment, promoted in part by regression-associated macrophages, as a therapeutically actionable node for extending the durability of response across oncogene-driven cancers. Significance: Natural killer cells recruited by regression-associated macrophages delay resistance to targeted therapies, highlighting the role of innate immune remodeling in targeted therapy durability and providing a strategy to prolong treatment efficacy.
— Source: Cancer Research Current Issue

item.title: [2.6] Dual-MEK Inhibitor Atebimetinib Displays Broad Activity in RAS - and RAF -Mutant Tumors via Deep Cyclic Inhibition and Resisting RAF Bypass
item.description:
Abstract Inappropriate activation of the mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) pathway, often stemming from activating mutations in RAS or RAF , represents one of the most common oncogenic events in human cancer. However, currently approved RAS/RAF inhibitors target specific mutants that are only present in a small proportion of RAS- or RAF-activated tumors. Current MEK inhibitors (MEKi) are associated with class-effect toxicities and tumor escape via CRAF bypass of MEK blockade. To address these issues, we designed atebimetinib to resist CRAF-mediated bypass and enable a pharmacokinetic/pharmacodynamic profile termed deep cyclic inhibition (DCI), an approach that transiently but deeply suppresses oncogenic signaling while allowing daily physiologic reset. Unlike chronic or intermittent approaches, DCI optimizes depth and duration of MEK suppression on a daily cycle, blunting rebound signaling while preserving recovery windows for normal tissues. Functioning as an allosteric, selective MEKi, atebimetinib potently inhibited ERK phosphorylation in vitro and in vivo , resisted CRAF bypass, and was well tolerated and more efficacious in xenograft models of cancer compared with current MEKis. Overall, these findings establish atebimetinib as a dual-MEKi with the potential to provide mutation-agnostic inhibition of the MAPK pathway while leveraging DCI, designed to avoid toxicities associated with existing MEKis. Atebimetinib offers MEK inhibition that is durable and tolerable, supporting the potential of this therapeutic paradigm. Significance: Atebimetinib, a deep cyclic inhibitor of MEK, blocks MAPK signaling, resists RAF bypass, and is active in RAS - and RAF -mutant tumors, representing a mechanistically differentiated approach in the field of targeted therapies. See related commentary by Gaire and Poulikakos, p. 5017
— Source: Cancer Research Current Issue

item.title: [1.5] SEZ6-Targeted PET Imaging and Alpha-Particle Radioimmunotherapy is Effective for Detection and Treatment of Small Cell Lung Cancer
item.description:
Abstract Small cell lung cancer (SCLC) remains one of the most lethal malignancies, with a 5-year survival of <10% despite advances in treatment. Seizure-related gene 6 (SEZ6), a type I transmembrane protein preferentially expressed in neuroendocrine tumors, has recently emerged as a promising therapeutic target, supported by clinical activity of SEZ6-targeted antibody–drug conjugates in relapsed SCLC. In this study, we developed and evaluated a humanized anti-SEZ6 monoclonal antibody for SEZ6-targeted positron emission tomography imaging and α-particle radioimmunotherapy. Immunohistochemistry of patient tissues confirmed strong, stage-independent SEZ6 expression. Cell-based studies demonstrated high SEZ6 receptor densities, supporting high-affinity antibody binding and rapid receptor-mediated internalization. [ 89 Zr]Zr-DFO-SEZ6-Ab administered at low antibody mass exhibited rapid hepatosplenic clearance with minimal tumor uptake despite high intratumoral levels. This pattern was consistent with active ectodomain shedding and local accumulation of soluble antigen within the tumor microenvironment, creating an extracellular antigen sink and limiting effective target engagement. Increasing the antibody mass overcame this barrier, dramatically increasing tumor uptake in xenografts. Treatment with [ 225 Ac]Ac-Macropa-SEZ6-Ab induced complete tumor regression, whereas coadministration of the ATR inhibitor berzosertib enhanced efficacy at lower radioactivity doses without added toxicity. Together, these findings identify tumor-localized SEZ6 shedding as a biological barrier to SEZ6-targeted therapy, define dosing strategies to overcome it, and demonstrate potent antitumor activity of SEZ6-directed α-particle radioimmunotherapy in SCLC. Significance: Dosing strategies that overcome antigen sink effects induced by a tumor-localized ectodomain shedding enable SEZ6-based imaging and theranostics in small cell lung cancer.
— Source: Cancer Research Current Issue

item.title: [2.6] Co-targeting KRAS and BCL-2 induces pyroptosis and antitumor tertiary lymphoid structures
item.description:
Mutant KRAS drives lung tumorigenesis through both cell-intrinsic and cell-extrinsic mechanisms, yet mutation subtype-specific differences in metabolic regulation and immune evasion remain incompletely understood. Here we show that the KRAS G12D mutation, particularly in the KRAS/STK11 co-mutant (KL) context, is associated with poor prognosis and a suppressed immune microenvironment characterized by impaired antigen presentation. At the cell-intrinsic level, G12D exhibits weakened interaction with hexokinase 1 (HK1), reduced spare respiratory capacity, and diminished mitochondrial stress resistance compared with G12C. Based on this mitochondrial vulnerability, we screened a panel of clinically available agents that induce mitochondrial stress and identified that co-targeting KRAS and BCL-2 synergistically triggers GSDME-mediated pyroptosis predominantly in G12D tumors. This combination further induces functional tertiary lymphoid structures (TLS) in vivo. Immune cell depletion experiments further demonstrate that the antitumor efficacy is dramatically dependent on B cells. Moreover, this treatment strategy induced membrane attack complex (MAC) deposition in situ and elicited memory antitumor responses. Collectively, these findings establish that combined KRAS and BCL-2 inhibition elicits pyroptosis and TLS formation, leading to B-cell-dependent in situ and memory antitumor immunity, providing a mechanistic rationale for targeting mitochondrial-immune crosstalk in KRAS G12D-mutant lung cancer.

item.title: [1.7] Chromosome 7 gain establishes a just-right WNT signaling state during colorectal tumorigenesis
item.description:
Aneuploidy is a hallmark of colorectal cancer, yet the functional consequences of recurrent chromosome gains and losses remain largely unknown. Leveraging advances in human colon organoid culture and chromosome copy number engineering, we here identify the gain of chromosome 7 as an adaptive event following APC loss-of-function mutation. Trisomy 7 confers a cell-intrinsic fitness advantage to APC-mutant colon organoids, while selective removal of the additional chromosome 7 copy from patient-derived colon cancer organoids severely impairs colorectal cancer organoid growth. By comparing transcriptomes of isogenic disomy 7 and trisomy 7 organoid lines, we found that chromosome 7 gain promotes organoid fitness through attenuation of excessive WNT-driven stemness caused by bi-allelic APC mutation. The gain of chromosome 7 thus establishes a just-right WNT signaling state. This effect of chromosome 7 gain is conserved from early adenoma-like APC-mutant organoids to advanced colorectal cancer organoids carrying additional oncogenic driver mutations. Moreover, consistent with our organoid data, gain of chromosome 7 is particularly common in tumors of colorectal cancer patients whose APC genotypes confer relatively high WNT activity. Overall, this work demonstrates that chromosome-specific aneuploidy can act as an adaptive mechanism to optimize, rather than maximize, oncogenic signaling during tumor evolution.

item.title: [1.8] Trp53 heterozygosity defines novel states impacting tumor plasticity and progression in Kras-initiated non-small cell lung cancer
item.description:
KRAS and TP53 are frequently mutated in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), the leading cause of cancer-related mortality worldwide. The most common event at the TP53 locus is mutation/loss of one allele and retention of a wild-type allele, which confers better survival outcomes than complete TP53 loss. To study the contribution of TP53 heterozygosity, we generated a murine lung tumor model with a KrasG12D mutation and intact (K) or single-allele loss (KP+/-) of Trp53 and compared it with publicly available complete loss (KP) data. K and KP+/- mice lived longer than KP mice, paralleling clinical survival data. Single-cell transcriptomic analysis of tumor-burdened lungs indicated that Trp53 heterozygosity expanded transcriptional plasticity that was not present in K and KP tumors. Genomic instability was also higher in KP+/- mice relative to the KP genotype. Trp53 gene dosage, thus, regulates phenotypic plasticity and evolutionary trajectories of tumor states across K, KP+/-, and KP tumors. Murine KP+/- tumor signatures and copy-number profiles were present in human NSCLC datasets. Two of these signatures correlated with better and worse patient survival outcomes, respectively. TP53 heterozygosity in KRAS-mutant lung cancers presents a distinct genomic landscape that should be taken into account in the development of novel therapeutic strategies.

item.title: [1.7] Microglia-derived Small Extracellular Vesicles Promote Bone Marrow Monocyte Expansion and Recruitment in Glioblastoma.
item.description:
Glioblastoma (GBM) remains one of the deadliest human cancers and is characterized by a profoundly immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment (TME). Although tumor-associated microglia (TAMg) promote GBM progression, their role in regulating immune cell recruitment remains poorly understood. Here, we demonstrate that TAMg-derived small extracellular vesicles (sEVs) mediate bone marrow-derived monocyte recruitment into the GBM TME. We find that these sEVs traffic to the bone marrow, where they selectively target monocytes and their progenitors. Mechanistically, sEV internalization activates MAPK signaling and inflammatory transcriptional programs, driving the differentiation and expansion of inflammatory monocytes. Together, our findings establish microglia-derived sEVs as a previously unrecognized mechanism of communication between the GBM TME and the peripheral immune system, thereby promoting the establishment of an immunosuppressive TME that drives GBM progression.
